Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • In a recent development, several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • The company declared Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

In a recent development, several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company declared Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it indicates can reach $15,000.

It has been revealed that the announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

According to recent reports, sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson stated in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

According to recent reports, compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it remarked already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the organization.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

It has been revealed that MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter stated.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

It has been revealed that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

According to recent reports, on Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the matter in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

According to recent reports, on Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He noted Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

Sources indicate that the dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

According to recent reports, amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS declared plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

According to recent reports, in an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton noted the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

Industry observers note that the growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Recent findings suggest that compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

Breaking: How State Environmental Laws Are Being ‘Weaponized’ To Stall Housing and Drive Up Costs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.
  • The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing.
  • The study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.

The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing. This comes as state lawmakers have proposed many new laws this year to curtail policies that stall building, with mixed success.

The study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws. Both of these kinds of disputes are expensive and time-consuming. Developers have to examine and reexamine the environmental impact of developments they want to build, and courts must then determine what cities are required to do to ensure a clean environment for residents.

"A real cost is borne on the people who are renting and buying those homes and apartments," Kyle Sweetland, the study's author, tells Realtor.com®.

About a dozen states have pitched laws that would make it easier to build homes, many of them by reducing zoning or lot size requirements. But some proposals have also met with failure, like California's Proposition 45, which aimed to expedite project reviews through the California Environmental Quality Act.

It has been revealed that the Realtor.com Housing Supply Gap research shows the U.S. faces a shortage of 4.03 million homes. Our Let America Build campaign has tracked how states have responded to this shortage, and which are tackling the problem.

It has been revealed that california has a long history of slow development on account of environmental review. In one recent example, a 49-unit housing development was stalled for 4.5 years in environmental litigation, which the developer mentioned had raised the cost of the project by $9 million. In another, a 34-home subdivision was stalled for nearly 40 years, in part because of neighbors' environmental concerns.

According to recent reports, it's not just a California problem. Sweetland looked at 16 states and the District of Columbia that have environmental policy acts that affect developers, or amendments that affect municipalities. Wyoming, Minnesota, New York, Hawaii, and Massachusetts have both.

But other protections are also in place in California, Nevada, Washington, North Dakota, Illinois, Wyoming, Michigan, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia.

It's hard to track precisely how much this kind of litigation drives up the costs of housing. Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner also notes that it's hard to tell how many housing projects didn't start in the first place because developers expected a lawsuit.

It has been revealed that "The bigger costs come from what the lawsuit does to the project’s financing and schedule," Berner says. "Appeals typically add years, and in the meantime, most projects can’t secure construction or grant funding. Loans, taxes, and insurance keep accruing, and construction costs can rise while the project waits.".

In a recent development, change could come at the federal level. Last week, the Senate passed a controversial bill that would reduce some federal environmental regulations, like the National Environmental Policy Act, to speed up construction of big-energy projects. Environmental groups opposed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which next heads to the House.

It has been revealed that in some instances, the environmental lawsuits don't actually produce better outcomes for the environment. Seattle found that just 16% of cases filed using environmental laws over the 2010s resulted in decisions requiring environmental remediation. In New York, about 22% of cases over 15 years resulted in more environmental reviews, an outside researcher found.

It has been revealed that berner says the balance is that environmental laws are sometimes the easiest avenue residents have to oppose a residential project. It's just a matter of not abusing the process.

"While challenging a project is a relatively cheap thing to do, being on the receiving end of a legal battle can derail a project even without going all the way through the litigation process," Berner indicates. "This uncertainty adds to the cost of capital for builders and squeezes out lower-margin projects like affordable and infill housing.".

In a recent development, pacific Legal Foundation says one solution for these challenges is to narrow the scope of some environmental laws. For instance, Sweetland says legal challenges from outside environmental groups could be limited. That way, the people challenging housing developments have a real vested interest in their outcomes.

Sources indicate that he also suggests requirements that groups that lose cases have to pay the legal fees. That isn't typical everywhere, even if developers pay the legal fees when they lose. That provides some incentive that those launching lawsuits have a legitimate claim, as opposed to using the courts as a stalling tactic.

"The law shouldn't just give anybody the ability to have a license to stop a building from moving forward," Sweetland states.

Recent findings suggest that tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

Regulated enterprises can now buy LigaData's data and governed AI through Google Cloud and run them wherever their data strategy requires, from the cloud to sovereign on-premises environments with LigaData's Barq Citadel.

PALO ALTO, Calif., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LigaData, a provider of data and governed AI for complex enterprise data in regulated industries, today announced that Data Flare, its data integration and preparation product, and LigaData Barq, its governed AI platform for management intelligence, are now available on Google Cloud Marketplace.

Recent findings suggest that ligaData software now processes 90 billion records a day across 27 countries for leaders across telecom, financial services, government and other regulated industries. Its products cover the path from raw data to governed AI: Data Platform, Data Flare, Data Governance and Barq. Data Flare prepares the data. Barq puts AI to work on it.

LigaData certified Data Flare and Barq on Google Cloud because BigQuery and Gemini are where enterprise data and AI are coming together.

Recent findings suggest that data Flare builds and runs the pipelines that bring data from separate systems into one consistent view, with one agreed definition of each business measure. Integration work that took months takes days. On Google Cloud it runs in the customer's own Google Kubernetes Engine cluster and writes to Cloud Storage, where BigQuery can query it without a separate load step. Every record is counted once, and every pipeline change goes through roles, approval and an audit trail.

Industry observers note that barq is the governed AI engine for management intelligence, working on the data an organization already has. Every answer traces back to the query and the source, and every request is checked against the customer's access rules. An answer can become a live application that keeps monitoring that part of the business, and external agents connect through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and APIs. No agent holds more authority than the person running it. Questions that took a data team three days to a week are answered in about 15 minutes.

Google Cloud customers can buy through their existing account with consolidated billing, and put AI to work on data already in BigQuery without moving it, using Gemini models through Vertex AI under their own access rules, masking and audit.

According to recent reports, "Our customers' data strategies don't fit a single deployment model. Some data has to stay on-premises under full sovereign control, and some belongs in the cloud," stated Shekhar Rajvanshy, Chief Engineering Officer, LigaData. "With Google Cloud, we can now meet them across that whole range with the same products. Governance is built into Data Flare and Barq, so the rules a customer sets apply the same way wherever these products run.".

In a recent development, ligaData is a Silicon Valley-based enterprise data and AI software tech giant and a member of the Google Cloud Partner Network. Learn more at ligadata.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:42 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Artificial intelligence developer ElevenLabs Inc. is reportedly in early talks to raise capital at a $33 billion valuation.

It has been revealed that bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the tech giant prepares to close the round in the first quarter of 2027. According to the report, some investors are pushing for the raise to happen sooner. That hints the planned round may include a secondary sale, a transaction that enables existing investors to cash out their shares.

It’s unclear how much ElevenLabs hopes to raise or from whom. Late-stage startup investments almost always include contributions from existing backers. ElevenLabs’ most recent raise, which valued it at $22 billion, saw the participation of Nvidia Corp.’s NVentures fund, Blackrock, Wellington and several others.

ElevenLabs’ fundraising push reportedly comes amid a surge in customer demand. Its annualized revenue is said to have grown by $100 million since September, to $700 million.

In a recent development, founded in 2022, ElevenLabs develops a series of AI models optimized to process audio. Companies use them to field call center inquiries, transcribe meetings, generate music and perform related tasks. It also offers a service called Productions that delivers ready-to-use audio assets.

It has been revealed that the company debuted its newest and most capable model, Eleven v4, in late September. The algorithm’s flagship feature is its ability to tailor its speaking style to each text snippet. It does so by automatically tuning parameters such as tone and pacing.

It has been revealed that users can manually customize Eleven v4’s speaking style by adding instructions to scripts. They can also generate conversations with multiple synthetic speakers. #157716. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

Industry observers note that for years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Industry observers note that we eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

Recent findings suggest that I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Industry observers note that once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

It has been revealed that what I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a fresh closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

Recent findings suggest that there’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Recent findings suggest that krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he noted.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Recent findings suggest that sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

According to recent reports, athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” mentioned Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively upcoming sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he stated, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

Sources indicate that what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he noted.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Recent findings suggest that often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

According to recent reports, but that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

According to recent reports, ATLANTA, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- PROPEL Center declared that the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff (UAPB) won the inaugural Future of XYZ HBCU Innovation Challenge at AfroTech, earning the $15,000 top prize for Brix, a money coaching app built by Gen Z for Gen Z. The win capped PROPEL's newest HBCU innovation challenge, which put student founders on a national technology stage during AfroTech week in Houston.

More than 30 historically Black colleges and universities applied to participate, with 10 finalist teams representing nine HBCUs advancing to the final round. Presented in partnership with AfroTech, the challenge culminated Nov. 2 and 3, with finalists presenting their ideas and pitching live to an audience of industry professionals. Future of XYZ is the newest chapter in PROPEL's innovation challenge series, following the Future of Tech earlier this year, which drew 1,100 applications from more than 80 HBCUs.

In a recent development, "HBCU students have never lacked talent. What they have too often lacked is access to the rooms, the resources and the relationships where talent gets backed," noted Harriette K. Burrell, President and Chief Strategy Officer of PROPEL Center. "PROPEL exists to open those rooms. From the Future of Tech to the Future of XYZ, we build the stages, the coaching and the industry connections that help students turn bold ideas into real ventures. The University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff just showed a national audience what happens when that access is real.".

The experience extended well beyond the final presentation. Over three weeks, participating students worked with PROPEL coaches and industry mentors with experience across business, engineering and other disciplines to refine their concepts, strengthen their presentations and sharpen their pitches. Students also attended a special breakfast hosted by Apple for the mentors and their students, where they connected with other industry professionals. Apple is PROPEL's Founding Partner.

Entergy, the Upcoming Orleansâbased energy company, served as a participating sponsor of the challenge in partnership with PROPEL.

Industry observers note that the winning team, UAPB students David Adedeji, Nicholas Nettey and Angel Yuzya, built Brix (usebrix.app), a money coaching app for first-generation and first-year students, designed for the moment money lands: a financial aid refund, a first paycheck, a first brokerage account. Its tagline is "Your money era starts here." Brix helps students spot the borrowed portion of a refund and its return window, build a plan that covers essentials first, and practice investing with fake money at real prices before putting real money at risk. In the team's own campus research, 66 percent of surveyed students had never bought a stock, 88 percent said their refund was gone or sitting untouched in the bank, and 74 percent wanted to practice first with fake money.

In a recent development, "Winning is an incredible honor, but the real prize is everything we gained along the way," remarked the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff's winning team. "The mentorship, the coaching and the chance to present Brix on a national stage challenged us to think bigger and communicate our vision with real confidence. We are leaving with more than a $15,000 prize. We are leaving with fresh skills, valuable connections and the belief that what we are building can make a real difference.".

Sources indicate that the Future of XYZ challenge continues the momentum of PROPEL's Future of Tech Innovation Challenge earlier this year, which brought 70 students to Austin, Texas, in April and awarded more than $120,000 in scholarships and prizes. Together, the challenges demonstrate how PROPEL is creating additional opportunities for HBCU students to showcase their talents while preparing for competitive professional environments.

For PROPEL, the value of these experiences is measured not only in prizes or pitches, but also in students' growth. Through targeted coaching, mentorship and exposure to industry leaders, participants develop communication, presentation, collaboration and other professional skills that help them translate innovation into opportunity.

The Future of XYZ HBCU Innovation Challenge at AfroTech is part of PROPEL's broader work to elevate HBCU talent, connect students with industry expertise and create pathways for the next generation of innovators and leaders.

PROPEL Center works to expand opportunities for HBCU students through innovation, experiential learning, mentorship and connections to industry. With Apple as its Founding Partner, PROPEL helps students develop the technical, entrepreneurial and professional capabilities to shape the future. To learn more, visit www.propelcenter.org.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sister will provide. True, French Gates stated, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

In a recent development, she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

It has been revealed that she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates noted she welcomed the conversation.

Sources indicate that “I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no.
  • Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Sources indicate that expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Industry observers note that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

It has been revealed that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

It has been revealed that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

Industry observers note that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Recent findings suggest that listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

In a recent development, twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

Sources indicate that we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

“It’s my job to put New York families first,” said Hochul, who explained as a mother and grandmother the matter is “deeply personal.” Hochul added that some of the wayward toys on the market at the moment have engaged children in “inappropriate conversations,” while some may also manipulate a child’s feelings or put their privacy at risk.

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Intersignal LLC today declared Braid 2.2, an update to its free local AI workspace that introduces named memory containers, reviewed memory bundles, searchable project context, and visible context budgets.

According to recent reports, braid connects local model conversations with project Channels, approved rig connections, an agent review Inbox, and built-in Folio publishing. Version 2.2 gives people a more organized way to preserve the mission, decisions, constraints, and next steps they want available in future conversations.

"Running a model on your own hardware is a powerful starting point. Keeping a project moving across conversations and computers is the next practical challenge," remarked David Seaman, founder of Intersignal. "Braid 2.2 lets people decide what is worth keeping, carry it between rigs, and inspect exactly what context their model was given.".

Give Each Mission a HomeMemory containers group related capsules within a Channel. Each capsule contains five editable fields: title, mission, decisions, constraints, and next steps.

According to recent reports, users can search capsule text, filter by container, and inspect the exact size of their selected memory context. A Channel can include up to four capsules within a 12,000-byte serialized context budget.

Recent findings suggest that saving memory and including it in chat remain separate choices. New and imported capsules start excluded. Customers select the capsules they want, enable the Channel's context permission, and choose whether to include that context in a chat request. Editing or moving a capsule clears its inclusion so the changed revision can be reviewed again.

Sources indicate that carry Reviewed Context Between RigsA complete container can be exported as a readable file and imported into another Channel or rig. The destination presents the container and every capsule's exact fields for review before confirmation.Confirmed imports receive upcoming local identities and start excluded from chat. Existing individual memory capsule files remain supported.

Industry observers note that memory files carry selected project context. They do not automatically synchronize computers, publish conversations, or grant permissions to connected AI clients. Chat receipts show the exact capsule revisions supplied to a model.

More Care for Work in ProgressBraid 2.2 also preserves unsent chat drafts when customers switch Channels within the same open window, asks before discarding changed memory fields, and saves capsule text and container changes together. Additional fixes guard against delayed responses changing the active conversation.

The release retains Braid's now familiar chat interface and text effect, reviewed agent proposals, approved rig handoffs, and Folio's workflow for shaping selected material into a public edition.

AvailabilityBraid 2.2 is available at https://intersignal.org/.Customers configure their model server and weights separately. Braid supports Ollama and local or LAN OpenAI-compatible inference endpoints, including servers provided by tools such as vLLM and LM Studio.

In a recent development, about IntersignalIntersignal LLC builds software for local AI, deliberate context sharing, and publishing under human control. Its Braid workspace brings local model conversations, project memory, rig connections, agent review, and Folio publishing into one application.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the tech giant’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Sources indicate that howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith stated on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

It has been revealed that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

It has been revealed that howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it released publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

According to recent reports, the deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

HelloNation has published an article featuring insights from Steve Lustig of Autosport Acura of Denville, explaining how certified pre-owned luxury vehicles may offer a practical balance between premium features and manageable long-term ownership costs.

It has been revealed that the article explains that many first-time buyers consider certified pre-owned luxury vehicles because they often provide advanced technology, premium interior materials, and modern safety systems at a lower purchase price than brand-latest models. According to the article, understanding how manufacturer certification programs work may help buyers feel more confident throughout the purchasing process and future luxury vehicle ownership experience.

One of the largest advantages discussed throughout the article is the inspection process required for certified pre-owned luxury vehicles. Many manufacturer programs require detailed multi-point inspections that evaluate major mechanical systems, electronics, brakes, tires, suspension components, and safety features before certification is approved. These inspections may help buyers feel more comfortable regarding vehicle reliability and overall condition.

Warranty coverage is another major topic highlighted in the article. Manufacturer-backed warranty coverage may provide protection for certain repairs and mechanical concerns after purchase. Compared to standard used vehicles without certification, certified pre-owned luxury vehicles often include more structured warranty coverage designed to reduce unexpected repair expenses during the ownership period. The article explains that carefully reviewing warranty coverage terms, duration, and limitations is an key step before making a purchase decision.

The HelloNation article also discusses the value of roadside assistance programs that are frequently included with manufacturer certification packages. Services such as towing support, flat tire assistance, battery service, and emergency roadside assistance may provide additional confidence for individuals entering luxury vehicle ownership for the first time. According to the article, roadside assistance programs often add value beyond the vehicle itself while helping drivers feel more prepared for unexpected situations.

According to recent reports, vehicle history reports are another important factor addressed throughout the article. Buyers are encouraged to review vehicle history reports carefully before purchasing certified pre-owned luxury vehicles. Accident history, previous ownership records, title status, and service information may all influence long-term reliability and resale value. Even when certification inspections have been completed, vehicle history reports remain an important tool for evaluating the overall condition and ownership background of a vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that maintenance records are also discussed as a key consideration for first-time buyers. Luxury vehicles often include specialized engineering and advanced performance systems that benefit from consistent service according to manufacturer recommendations. Reviewing maintenance records may help buyers confirm whether oil changes, brake service, tire maintenance, and other scheduled services were completed properly over time. Certified pre-owned luxury vehicles with strong maintenance records may provide greater confidence regarding long-term reliability.

The article further explains that technology features continue to attract many buyers to certified pre-owned luxury vehicles. Modern luxury vehicles often include premium sound systems, advanced infotainment platforms, driver assistance technology, navigation systems, and upgraded safety features. Purchasing certified pre-owned models may allow drivers to access these premium technologies at a more manageable overall cost.

Sources indicate that long-term ownership costs are another key consideration discussed throughout the article. While certified models may reduce initial purchase expenses compared to new vehicles, buyers should still evaluate insurance costs, future maintenance expectations, tire replacement expenses, and potential repair needs. Understanding warranty coverage, maintenance records, and manufacturer certification standards may help buyers make more informed luxury vehicle ownership decisions.

The article concludes that carefully reviewing inspection standards, vehicle history reports, roadside assistance programs, maintenance records, and warranty coverage may help first-time buyers better understand the long-term value of certified pre-owned luxury vehicles.

  • It has been revealed that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

It has been revealed that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

Recent findings suggest that “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont mentioned in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon mentioned in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

Recent findings suggest that “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

According to recent reports, the solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

In a recent development, “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel stated. “I think it’s notable to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

In a recent development, tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

It has been revealed that “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really crucial component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker mentioned. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

It has been revealed that the startup mentioned today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really substantial step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

According to recent reports, nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Sources indicate that boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

In a recent development, long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles mentioned. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

It has been revealed that retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Sources indicate that next year, Zeno Power prepares to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

"Our guests aren't simply purchasing a vacation," Glenn concluded. "They are investing in memories they will cherish for the rest of their lives. UPDATED 21:52 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?

In a recent development, identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question. The internet and mobile disrupted the landscape by bringing more people and devices onto the network, but the underlying problem remained.

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence agents expose the limits of that question. An agent can hold only the permissions it was given and still email a customer list to a stranger because it read an instruction buried on a web page or in a support ticket and treated it as a legitimate order. That is the problem Cato Networks Ltd. is trying to solve with its recent launch of AgentSense, a runtime capability built into its secure access service edge platform.

Recent findings suggest that agentSense monitors an agent as it works and traces each proposed action back to its instruction source. Its first component, Untrusted Influence Detection, separates what the user asked for from content the agent encounters along the way, such as emails, documents and tool responses. If that external content steers the agent toward a risky step, the action is blocked before it runs. A second component, Drift Detection, is planned to check whether an agent’s steps still serve its original task.

With agentic agents, they can have the right permissions and still take harmful actions. The first release covers coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot. These are included at no extra charge in Cato AI Usage licenses, and Cato is offering $10,000 to each of the first three researchers who can beat it. This has clear value for security leaders. As organizations give AI more responsibility, they need visibility into what it is doing and when human intervention is required.

Sources indicate that language models read instructions and data in the same stream, and no patch will change that. Filters that look for known attack phrases catch poorly formed attempts, but a well-written injection will be interpreted as a valid business request. The control therefore must sit at the moment of action and ask where the instruction came from.

According to recent reports, permissions alone won’t close the gap because multiple actions, when executed individually, can still combine to produce an unauthorized outcome. Adoption is far ahead of control. A Gartner survey cited by Fierce Network found that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have governance in place.

It has been revealed that agentSense is a single product from a single vendor, and it will take time and independent testing to prove itself. The more important point is the shift it represents. Zero trust taught us to verify who is asking. Agents also require us to verify why an action is happening and whose instruction is behind it.

Recent findings suggest that the companies that get value from agents will be the ones that can let them run without watching every step, and that only happens when the controls are in place first. Start the inventory and the permission cleanup now. The tools to enforce the rest are arriving swiftly, and they will work far better for the teams that did the groundwork.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with massive financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • Recent findings suggest that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with massive financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

Recent findings suggest that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Recent findings suggest that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

Recent findings suggest that for Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond firm agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

In a recent development, listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old tech giant was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei stated Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he noted.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.
