Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • Sources indicate that the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

Sources indicate that the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the firm acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

According to recent reports, testing that more closely replicates the firm’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

Sources indicate that what set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software upgrade that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

In a recent development, the bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows upgrade used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

In a recent development, so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July enhancement was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report indicates.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

According to recent reports, second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

Sources indicate that how it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report claims.

Recent findings suggest that the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

It has been revealed that once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It has been revealed that it also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

In a recent development, some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft notes its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it intends to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

In a recent development, the report also confirms what Microsoft noted the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it claims. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

Sources indicate that the fresh testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the firm says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

Industry observers note that david Schwartz, CTO Emeritus at Ripple and one of the creators of the XRP Ledger, has once again commented on his XRP and Bitcoin sales. This time, the reason was a viral post on X that claimed he had sold almost all of his crypto over the last few months.

In a recent development, according to the post, Schwartz's portfolio reportedly went from 26 million XRP, 1,500 BTC and 40,000 ETH to just 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH. The author called it "an insane reduction" and also referred to Schwartz as the current CTO of Ripple, while he now holds the emeritus title.

Schwartz replied that the timeline in the post was wrong. "That wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade," he wrote. As proof, he shared his own post from April 21, 2019. In that post, Schwartz said he was still sticking to the "de-risking strategy" that he and his wife agreed on when they first decided to put their own money into crypto. He also admitted back then that selling during the bull run "still hurt.".

Sources indicate that at the same time, Schwartz did not dispute the numbers themselves. "But it's basically true. I hate risk. I can't help it," he wrote in a follow-up post. According to him, pretty much every big risk he has ever taken has worked out well, and rationally he should be taking more risk as he gets wealthier. "But I hate it. I just hate risk and can't do anything about it," Schwartz added.

According to recent reports, that wasn't in the last few months, that was in the last decade. You can find me talking about this in many posts over the years, like this one:https://t.co/5MgcPZ5qyG.

At press time, XRP was trading at around $0.939, Bitcoin at $61,477 and Ethereum at $1,722. At these prices, the remaining 3 million XRP, 1 BTC and 6 ETH are worth about $2.89 million, and XRP accounts for more than 97% of this sum.

For comparison, at current prices, the peak holdings mentioned in the post would be worth over $185 million, with Bitcoin alone accounting for about half of it.

In a recent development, schwartz has already explained his sales several times this year. In May, he remarked he did not have much XRP left and had tried to move most of his assets, other than Ripple stock, away from crypto exposure. In July, he said he regrets selling XRP at $0.10 and ETH at around $1, but noted that he and his wife had agreed to sell at every new all-time high.

In a recent development, earlier in November, Schwartz disclosed that he sold about 2.5 million XRP in 2025. Per Schwartz, most of these tokens were received in 2020 and 2023, and he paid approximately $1.7 million in capital gains tax on those sales. He shared this in response to a user who called XRP a "terrible investment.".

It has been revealed that among other things, Schwartz has previously said that his main exposure to the crypto sector now comes through Ripple stock, not XRP. In March, Ripple launched a share buyback of up to $750 million that valued the company at $50 billion.

#157642. Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1026 w)

Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless.
  • Sources indicate that few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa.
  • She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless. She knows about the hole-in-the-wall restaurant before the line wraps around the block, has a vacation wardrobe worth taking notes on, and somehow finds time to read the book everyone will be talking about in six months.

Sources indicate that few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa. The Grammy-winning pop star has become as much an inspiration for where to vacation, what to read, and where to eat as for what to listen to.

She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.

But after years of celebrities turning their personalities into businesses and influencers making nearly every aspect of their lives shoppable, the economics of being cool may be changing. Being everywhere may no longer make someone worth following, which poses a slight problem for an industry that makes money off visibility.

U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion this year, more than triple the $13.9 billion spent in 2021, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. But even as brands pour more money into the creator economy, younger consumers are growing weary of its biggest stars.

A July survey of 13- to 39-year-olds from youth research firm YPulse found that 62% are tired of seeing the same massive names everywhere, while 73% trust smaller creators more than big influencers.

“You can pay for attention, but you can’t buy cultural credibility or this idea of being cool,” Izzy Farmiloe, global head of strategy and growth at Dazed Studio, the agency arm of youth culture and fashion publisher Dazed Media, told Fortune.

Long before Instagram gave celebrities a place to document their breakfast, much of the fascination with the cool girl came from how little the public knew about her.

According to recent reports, in a November essay for his newsletter, Considered Chaos, brand strategist Eugene Healey explained how each generation’s cool girl was shaped by the media of her time. Kate Moss had fashion magazines, the Olsen twins had the paparazzi, and Alexa Chung had fashion blogs and street-style photographers.

Social media brought audiences closer to the women they admired, making relatability an asset for personalities like Emma Chamberlain. As algorithms began serving up content based on people’s interests rather than simply who they followed, celebrities also had more reason to venture beyond the industries that made them famous.

“Dua Lipa was made for the feed,” Healey wrote.

It has been revealed that her friendship with designer Simon Porte Jacquemus might draw in fashion enthusiasts, while her book club could introduce her to someone who has never listened to Future Nostalgia. Each new audience offers another opportunity to make money beyond selling records and concert tickets.

Sources indicate that it’s a business model that has become increasingly familiar, with celebrities launching beauty brands, starting newsletters, and inviting followers into their kitchens. Somewhere along the way, having a favorite lip gloss became an opportunity to launch a cosmetics company.

In a recent development, the trouble with making a living off being cool is that the more people see someone being paid to recommend things, the harder it becomes to tell what she actually likes. Even the seemingly casual Instagram photo dump, filled with blurry pictures and half-eaten meals, can be as carefully curated as the polished posts it was meant to replace.

For Jenna Drenten, a marketing professor at Loyola University Chicago, the problem lies in the very nature of an influencer’s job. “They are expected to sell what is popular, but also expected to discover what’s new,” Drenten told Fortune.

In a recent development, drenten pointed to BookTok, where recommending a novel outside the usual bestseller rotation can set a creator apart. If enough people take her advice, however, the book becomes just another BookTok sensation, losing some of the very appeal that made it worth recommending in the first place.

According to recent reports, brands risk falling into the same trap. Farmiloe has seen companies chase the same trends and hire the same talent in their pursuit of relevance, spending money only to end up looking more like one another.

“I actually think silence can often be a stronger strategy now,” Farmiloe noted.

Trying too hard to look polished may also backfire for brands, especially as artificial intelligence makes it easier to produce everything from flawless images to cultural recommendations. “To sort of show mistakes is a way of proving that a human has made something,” Farmiloe said, adding that even typos have become chic.

Healey identified three potential successors to the Dua Lipa era: the obsessive, who knows a particular subject inside and out; the ghost, whose reputation spreads without constantly posting; and the host, who brings people together in real life.

He argued that the three share expertise and charisma that are hard to fake at a moment when faking has never been easier. If the next dominant medium is an AI model that can summarize the world’s knowledge on demand, Healey wrote, cool becomes whatever can’t be summarized.

It has been revealed that for brands accustomed to measuring influence in followers, likes, and views, the next cool girl may be much harder to price. Drenten sees growing appeal in people who can offer something beyond a product recommendation, whether it’s a longtime librarian who can introduce readers to literature they might never have discovered on their own or someone who brings strangers together outside the confines of their carefully curated feeds.

As going out becomes increasingly expensive, Farmiloe sees an opportunity for brands to help create those experiences. She pointed to Reference Point, a London library, bookshop, and bar that doubles as a gathering place for chess, poetry, and jazz.

Rather than paying someone to talk about a brand, companies could give people a place to spend time together.

“Instead of just getting noticed, how do you get people to care or actually like engage or spend time with your brand?” Farmiloe said.

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley, a GeekWire contributing writer, sizes up where the firm stands after one of its most eventful weeks in years.

Sources indicate that microsoft opened its Ignite conference with an apology for the global Outlook outage, then took direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic on price, even though it invests in both and sells their models. We discuss the lasting damage from the outage, why enterprise customers have few places to go even when they’re fed up, and Microsoft’s pitch to make Copilot the “OS for work,” as Anthropic goes public.

Plus, we weigh who from Microsoft could lead Nvidia, and the GeekWire trivia challenge goes back to 1997.

Cardano just saw a death cross on its daily chart, with the 50 MA falling below the 200 MA. The timing of this signal remains significant, as it marks the second consecutive November in the last two years that Cardano has marked a death cross. Cardano saw a death cross in November 2025, and the same is happening this November.

Recent findings suggest that the signal in November 2025 was followed by months of falling prices, which has led some to speculate that the cryptocurrency may have further downside or a recovery ahead of the end of 2026. The current uncertainty in the market has added to concerns. A volatile weekend saw Cardano fall as low as $0.134, its weakest level since December 2020, before rebounding. This recovery has entered its third day, with ADA up 2.05% in the last 24 hours to $0.146.

Whether that rebound holds is the test traders will keep an eye on. The $0.18 area represents an initial resistance level, while a stronger recovery toward the $0.198 to $0.20 range would bring Cardano closer to its daily moving averages.

According to recent reports, another possibility is sideways trading as ADA attempts to establish a sustainable bottom. Its daily RSI is flirting with oversold territory that may trigger a relief bounce, but that’s not enough to confirm a trend reversal. In a bearish scenario, continued selling pressure could push ADA below its recent $0.134 support area, exposing lower price levels.

In a recent development, crypto markets head into a holiday-shortened U.S. week with inflation data that could shape how big a rate increase the Federal Reserve will consider next month. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, is due Wednesday and is expected to show prices rose 0.3% in October after a 0.5% gain in September.

Five different node implementations have now produced blocks on Cardano mainnet. Protocol version 12 testing continues on Musashi and Dijkstra (11.2.1 Pre-release) testnets.

Work progresses on a node version 11.2.x with Mainnet clearance; until then, 11.1.3 remains the recommended version. Node 11.2.0 introduced a upcoming “envelope” config file format, which will be the format published on the config file pages for networks running 11.2.0 and above.

UPDATED 10:00 EST / NOVEMBER 27 2026.

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof.

Jensen Huang’s back, and not everyone is happy with that.

Nvidia’s board reversed the resignation of its former and current-again CEO Monday, apparently under pressure from the well-known business genius and lame-duck President Donald Trump, who worried that the stock market and the AI trade would suffer without him at the helm.

Industry observers note that huang (pictured) clearly has management talent, having built one of the most valuable companies in the world. But his return, amid continuing revelations and questions about Nvidia’s business, sets an awful precedent in business. No one person should be too important to fail, and Huang set up a corporate structure that courts disaster if he’s forced to leave again or gets run over by a bus. That’s a world-class failure of a CEO and his board at one of their most basic jobs, and his tech-bro enablers should know better than to clamor for his return.

After all, internal and government investigations continue, as more details come to light about probably the worst of the whole affair(s). It’s clear that at a time when there’s existential worry about China closing the U.S. lead in AI — a potential defense and cybersecurity disaster — the chief supplier of AI chips was allowing cutting-edge chips to be sent to China. Oh, and this week’s stock market pretty much discounted much of the supposed benefit Huang’s reinstatement was supposed to provide.

It has been revealed that so what are we left with? The CEO of the pivotal firm in AI is back with not even a slap on the wrist, let alone any consequences for multiple affairs — one with a woman who shuttled both barred GPUs and apparently inside information to China, another with an Nvidia VP, plus at least a couple others he fessed up to. Oh, and he lied about them until he couldn’t anymore. Any semblance of corporate governance and ethics — at Nvidia and everywhere else by example — is utterly torched.

According to recent reports, hey, if you think that’s a buying opportunity, I’ve got some high-end GPUs in Singapore to sell you. Anyway, let’s move on before I tell you what I really think.

Paul Gillin dove into why open-weight AI models that enterprises can tailor to their specific needs are taking off this year. “The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management,” he notes. “Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task.”.

Last week Palo Alto Networks said it will acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. This week was CrowdStrike’s turn, as it pulled the trigger on buying Zscaler for a pretty stunning $44 billion. As AI makes cyberattacks far easier and more numerous, it seems a sure bet that today’s rickety cybersecurity industry with hundred of point products won’t stand.

It has been revealed that AI continues to be a significant driver of upside earnings surprises, but investors increasingly wary of AI spending are all over the place. Dell in particular more than doubled its revenue, only to see its shares go nowhere Wednesday, while HP got hit by the PC slowdown but saw its shares rise more than 12%. Likewise, HPE’s stock slid despite an upbeat forecast.

Next week, look for earnings from Salesforce, Snowflake, UiPath, Marvell, MongoDB, NetApp, Okta and more.

But the big news next week will be AWS re:Invent, which customarily releases dozens of newly introduced services at its re:Invent conference in Las Vegas. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE Research, theCUBE, along with tens of thousands of attendees, will be onsite and we’ll have all the news, analysis and interviews.

Here’s all of the Thanksgiving-shortened week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:.

Trump has found something to blame for his midterm loss: ‘Fake’ growth numbers out of Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the headaches just keep piling up for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
  • “The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.”.
  • The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the headaches just keep piling up for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been on his case about the Commerce Department’s handling of Nvidia, following the news of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. And now President Trump is blaming his team for publishing “fake” growth numbers before the midterms.“It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers,” the president posted on Truth Social.

“The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.”.

The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.

The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics.

On Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.”.

Analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan noted in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of annualization (a technique employed by very few advanced economies).”.

“Data revisions are more common as structural change and poor survey response rates reduce precision.”.

But President Trump suggested there were more nefarious reasons for the near-percentage-point difference in initial estimates to the published figures: “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error.”.

Lutnick issued a bullish economic enhancement. Writing on X, the Commerce Secretary noted: “We’re bringing American manufacturing back at a scale nobody thought possible. America’s successes will become even more powerful in the coming years as these projects move from groundbreaking to full production.”.

In a recent development, trump’s latest clash with federal data agencies could further undermine confidence in U.S. economic statistics. In 2025, the president fired the director of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Erika McEntarfer, claiming she had overseen the publishing of “phony” job numbers for political reasons. (The president provided no evidence for his claim.).

Recent findings suggest that this, paired with Trump’s extraordinary attacks on the Federal Reserve under former chairman Jerome Powell, led many economists and investors to worry about the credibility of major U.S. institutions that either inform policy or make it.

At the time, Alberto Cavallo, Professor at Harvard Business School, told Goldman Sachs: “It’s difficult to avoid a comparison to the experience of my home country, Argentina, nearly two decades ago when the president, dismayed at rising inflation, removed statistical agency leadership.

“Some statistics stopped being reported, and official data no longer seemed to align with perceptions. That was a very chaotic period that destroyed trust in Argentina’s official statistics for over a decade.”.

While Cavallo said the U.S. is ahead of some of Argentina’s data bodies in terms of skills and institutional checks and balances, he said the situation was still “very concerning.”.

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • Sources indicate that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • In a recent development, attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

Sources indicate that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

In a recent development, attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals concern ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

It has been revealed that each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal patch at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

Sources indicate that A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

In a recent development, last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella notes his firm’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he stated at the Latest York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

Industry observers note that the FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t update for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

Sources indicate that there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

According to recent reports, former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Amid growing market fear, Ethereum outflows from Binance over the last month have hit a historic low as investors continue to move fewer ETH tokens away from the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As demand for major crypto assets has increased, Ethereum remains on hold amid growing market fear and uncertainty, while exchange activities across the broad crypto market are showing a bearish trend.

While Ethereum remains one of the most affected cryptocurrencies during the prolonged crypto market volatility, the latest data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant reveals a massive slowdown in its exchange outflows.

Amid growing market fear, Ethereum outflows from Binance over the last month have hit a historic low as investors continue to move fewer ETH tokens away from the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.

The data indicates that about 3.58 million ETH have been withdrawn from Binance over the last 30 days, marking an all-time low in Ethereum outflows on the exchange.

Further data shows that the decline has come as Ethereum continues to struggle to stabilize its price and continues to weaken, trading around the $1,700 mark.

It is important to note that the decline in exchange outflows is expected, considering the growing market weakness and negative shift in investor sentiment over the period.

However, the metric has drawn different attention from market participants, given expectations that the massive security breach Binance suffered should trigger large withdrawals from the exchange.

Although blockchain trackers recently identified multiple large Ethereum withdrawals by the Binance hacker, it appears that the moves did not materialize into increased Ethereum outflows.

Apart from the attackers' withdrawals, it appears that Ethereum holders on the exchange did not respond to the attack in the conventional way, as security incidents like this often make investors more cautious and wary about keeping their assets on the exchange.

While this typically prompts them to transfer the assets into private wallets where they have greater control, it appears that Ethereum holders remained comfortable with keeping their funds on the exchange.

#157630. Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (838 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips 📈 Bullish 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback.
  • Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it.
  • On November 12, Nvidia declared that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation, after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored.

I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every organization whose CEO looks irreplaceable.

The sequence of events tells a story.

On November 12, Nvidia declared that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation, after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board remarked it would consider internal and external candidates.

Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.”.

Then the alternatives fell away. The Financial Times reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day, Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government. Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision.

The board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished.

Industry observers note that that’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that says no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options.

A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse.

Industry observers note that accountability depends on a credible alternative. When a board has a successor ready, its questions carry weight, because everyone in the room knows the company survives if the answers fall short. When it has nobody, the CEO holds the leverage and both sides know it. The duty to oversee him turns into a duty to keep him.

According to recent reports, huang has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993. The board had three decades to prepare for the day he wasn’t there. When that day came, it had a CFO doing two jobs, one outside name, and a market that wanted him back. Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld wrote in Fortune the board had no Proposal B.

It has been revealed that investors made the same point from the other side. Within days of the resignation, prominent shareholders were urging the board to keep the door open to Huang. Nobody outside the firm had the facts. What they were pricing was a business with no one else to run it.

Sources indicate that the board has since created a national security committee and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Those are controls on conduct. Neither one is a successor.

Sources indicate that I coach CEOs, and I’ve watched how boards arrive here. Nobody decides to skip succession. It gets postponed, one good quarter at a time.

In a recent development, over the years a founder’s identity and the organization’s fuse. Raising the question of who comes next starts to feel like disloyalty, so directors leave it for another meeting. The CEO rarely pushes either. Planning your own exit means picturing a company that no longer needs you, and that is the hardest thing to ask of someone whose whole identity is the company.

According to recent reports, so both sides stay comfortable. The cost arrives on the one day the board needs a choice and finds it doesn’t have one.

Plenty of boards are living with the same arrangement right now, and it’s invisible for as long as the results are good.

Two tests will tell a director where their board stands.

Industry observers note that first, name the person who could run the company on Monday. One name, already inside the building, whom the top team would follow. If the honest answer is the CFO as caretaker, you have a holding pattern.

Industry observers note that second, recall the last time the board said no to the CEO on something he cared about. If nobody can remember one, the board has already stopped overseeing him. It just hasn’t been tested yet.

According to recent reports, huang may prove to be the right leader for Nvidia’s next chapter. The investigation may answer every open question. Neither would change what the 11 days highlighted.

The board now enters the next crisis in a weaker position than the last one. It has shown its investors, its government and its CEO that it has no alternative to him. He knows it. So does everyone who will ever need to challenge him.

Every director reading this should ask the question Nvidia’s board had to answer in public.

If our CEO were gone tomorrow, would we have a choice?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one rather unusual metric on XRP Ledger has seen more than a 3,062% increase in usage which raises a lot of questions. This is one of the largest spikes throughout the year in a function usage that mostly stays low.

The function allows people to manage their secondary keys for signing transactions on their wallets and/or accounts. Their main private keys stay offline, while a certain key issued by them is used in daily transactions.

It allows safer work and utilization of their wallets without potentially exposing their private keys. So even if someone grabs hold of your signing credentials, you'll be able to protect your funds by nullifying the issued keys, provided you still retain authorized access.

In a recent development, one way or another, the surge is bizarre. Most likely "legit" scenarios are: automated key rotations among large custodians like exchanges. Some security warnings that triggered massive migration and then, the illicit one: generation of function calls from bots or automated scripts.

The flatlined chart actually represents tens or hundreds of calls daily, but a surge to nearly 4,000 is certainly out of the blue. Unfortunately, we were unable to identify the source of those transactions.

The feature itself is legitimate, so the spike alone does not indicate that consumers' funds or wallets are at risk. However, an undisclosed exploit or security glitch cannot be ruled out without further investigation.

Industry observers note that one concerning scenario would involve malicious actors gaining access to wallets and assigning upcoming regular keys to maintain control over them. This would not necessarily mean that the XRP Ledger itself has been compromised, but rather that individual accounts may have been targeted.

For now, there is no evidence pointing toward such an attack, and the activity could just as easily be attributed to routine security operations.

Still, XRP holders should keep an eye on any unexpected changes to their account settings, especially regular keys they did not authorize.

Whether this was a coordinated security upgrade, automated activity, or something more concerning remains unclear. What is certain is that such an unusual spike deserves closer attention, particularly if similar activity continues over the coming days.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tesla has pulled the $41,990 Model Y All-Wheel Drive from its US online configurator. The cheapest dual-motor Model Y you can order now is the Model Y Premium AWD at $49,990, an $8,000 jump.

It has been revealed that the trim lasted just over nine months. Tesla launched it in early February, and it’s gone without a word from the company.

Here’s what Tesla’s US Model Y design studio lists as of today (prices before the destination fee):.

When Tesla launched the base Model Y AWD in February, it was basically the stripped-down Model Y with a second motor. It had 294 miles of range, did 0-60 mph in 4.6 seconds and kept the same cut-down cabin as the base RWD. At a $2,000 premium over the single-motor version, it was the most sensible AWD pricing Tesla had offered in years.

Sources indicate that and the AWD trim isn’t the only change. In February, the Premium RWD cost $44,990 and the Premium AWD cost $48,990. Both are now $1,000 higher.

Add it up and the cheapest all-wheel-drive Model Y went from $41,990 to $49,990 in nine months. That’s a 19% increase.

The timing isn’t great for Tesla’s competitive position. Chevrolet’s 2027 Equinox EV LT 1 AWD starts at $40,295 before destination, with 307 miles of EPA range. Ford’s Mustang Mach-E Select AWD starts at $40,795.

Both now undercut Tesla’s cheapest AWD crossover by more than $9,000.

Industry observers note that if you live somewhere it snows and you were shopping for a new Model Y, the math just got a lot worse. You can still find some base AWD units in Tesla’s inventory, but once those are gone, that’s it.

This is also the latest cut in a year of Tesla shrinking its lineup. Elon Musk killed the Model S and Model X in January to free up Fremont for Optimus, and Cybertruck production is winding down. Meanwhile, the most recent new Tesla is the $61,990 Model Y L, which sits at the top of the range, not the bottom.

Industry observers note that we liked this trim. It was the first time in a long time that Tesla treated all-wheel drive as a $2,000 option rather than a huge upsell bundled with a nicer interior, and it put the Model Y right in the price bracket of the Equinox EV and Mach-E with AWD.

In a recent development, now it’s gone, and the Premium trims went up $1,000 on top of that. Tesla didn’t explain either move. It rarely does anymore.

In a recent development, there are two plausible reasons. Either Tesla is tight on Model Y build slots and would rather fill them with higher-margin Premium trims, or the cheap AWD simply wasn’t selling. We don’t know which. But both explanations land in the same place for buyers: a more expensive Model Y.

It has been revealed that tesla is not going to keep 6 different model Y trims especially when the most expensive trim in the Model YL is selling. They will definitely squeeze out as much money from selling more expensive trims so the lowest end trim will most likely be next to go.

According to recent reports, and Tesla has a habit of this. The “Standard” name for its cheaper Model Y and Model 3 lasted a few months. The single-motor Cybertruck, the only version that made sense, was gone within days. Cheaper trims show up, get a news cycle, and quietly disappear.

That’s a problem for a firm whose consumer lineup is shrinking down to two cars. The Model Y is Tesla’s volume. Thinning it out at the bottom is the opposite of what you’d do if growing EV sales were the priority.

Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • It has been revealed that the outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

It has been revealed that the outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

In a recent development, the fresh funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of substantial names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the tech giant-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that “The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis remarked the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight tech giant acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders stated the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis mentioned.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The firm cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders noted. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

It has been revealed that both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The manufacturer notes it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

In a recent development, srinivasan said that at the major tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a latest AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he mentioned.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The manufacturer’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

It has been revealed that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe intends to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

Recent findings suggest that the $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis mentioned. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

According to recent reports, past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis noted the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis remarked he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of fresh chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

According to recent reports, updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

In 2026, many employers are ditching merit-based pay bumps in favor of ‘peanut butter raises’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow.
  • It has been revealed that around 44% of employers initiative to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report.
  • Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend.

It has been revealed that around 44% of employers initiative to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report. About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases.

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the latest compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers.

Recent findings suggest that “Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a massive concern.”.

Job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty.

According to recent reports, wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “K-shaped economy”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment.

While U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson, there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses strategy to lower their compensation-increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs.

Last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks declared it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader manufacturer turnaround effort.

According to recent reports, but Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard.

“Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke mentioned, as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.”.

According to recent reports, as more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart, unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year.

U.S. CEO John Furner remarked it was a way to “make managers feel like owners,” acknowledging their success with a slice of the profit pie. Their average base pay was hiked from $130,000 to $160,000, raising their total compensation to between $420,000 and $620,000 annually.

Sources indicate that and with more than 4,000 store managers across the U.S. (and around 1.5 million workers) when the policy went into effect, the payout wasn’t just generous—it was a calculated bet on culture.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on February 2, 2026.

Long-time Shiba Inu community member and SHIB developer, Mazrael, has reacted to Solana-based memecoin platform Pump.fun's recent wallet login changes, which are sparking concerns about private key security.

Sources indicate that in a new announcement, Pump.fun stated that external wallet sign-in is being retired on November 30, 2026. Starting November 30, 2026 (15:00 UTC), Pump.fun on the web will only allow users to sign in with an email account or a Google, Apple, or GitHub account instead of an external wallet such as Phantom, Solflare, or Ledger.

Pump.fun reassures users that nothing will happen to their funds or account, as their wallet address, positions, callouts, followers and username remain unchanged. The only change is how users sign in.

Users who sign in to their accounts with Phantom or any other wallet are urged to take action before the November 30, 2026 deadline.

In a recent development, pump.fun outlined a number of steps for users on how to switch their sign-in; of particular concern is the step that asked users to enter their wallet details and paste their private key when prompted. Pump.fun noted that this step encrypts the key in the user's browser and that the key is end-to-end encrypted by its login provider, Privy, allowing users' wallets to continue working for everything else.

Mazrael reacted to the development, drawing attention to the potential security implications for owners.

Recent findings suggest that pumpfun is retiring external wallet logins on web starting Nov 30. From then on you sign in with Google, Apple, email or GitHub. To keep your existing account..... they want you to paste your private key into their Privy flow 😬 Also note their own terms says they won’t ask for private keys...

In a recent development, the standard security practice across the cryptocurrency industry is that exchanges, wallet providers and other platforms do not ask users to disclose their private keys or recovery phrases. Such warnings are routinely issued to protect users from unauthorized access to their funds.

The Pump.fun wallet login change process appears to contradict this widely promoted security principle, Mazrael noted.

According to recent reports, private keys are highly sensitive credentials that give holders direct access to their cryptocurrency wallets. Whoever gets their hands on them might be able to access those wallets and move the funds. In general, it is recommended never to share private keys with individuals, support agents or third-party services.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a 2026 Gartner survey, 87% of customers stated companies using generative AI for customer service must provide access to a human agent.

That doesn’t mean customers are against AI. It means businesses need to think carefully about where they use it and where human support still matters.

Every business was built on a dream, and that’s a deeply human thing. When we replace real care with automation in the moments that matter most, we risk chipping away at the very thing that made the business worth building.

So how do you know where AI belongs and which moments need protecting? Start by asking four questions, then test your answers.

Before using AI in any area of your business, ask these four questions:.

If a behind-the-scenes task is predictable, simple and low-stakes, let AI handle it. If it’s personal, complex or high-stakes, keep a person in the loop.

Recent findings suggest that I recently heard from an AnswerConnect client, Craig Grove, founder of GRT Realty, who learned the hard way where not to put AI. He partnered with an AI answering service, only to realize his leads were hanging up on the robot. After switching to human phone answering, he grew his business from six real estate agents to 70.

In a recent development, running the four questions tells you where AI could go. Testing tells you whether it’s actually working.

I’ve learned firsthand that even the best ideas benefit from a little testing before they’re rolled out more widely. I’m naturally someone who likes to take action, particularly when I’m confident something has potential. After a few instances where the direction or idea I had in mind wasn’t as great as I thought, I found myself in a place where I’d made mistakes.

Recent findings suggest that in hindsight, I should have started smaller, talked to more people and got feedback first. I’ve never regretted taking a little extra time to test an idea before jumping in. AI deserves the same approach.

Look at it from two angles: your customers and your team.

Industry observers note that then make testing a habit. Things are constantly changing, including your customers’ expectations. What worked in January can fail by June.

Industry observers note that AI is one of the most useful tools business owners have ever had. Used in the right place, it gives your people more time for the work that matters. Used in the wrong place, it erodes the trust your business was built on.

So ask the four questions, test the answers, and keep checking.

Industry observers note that your business was built on a dream. Use AI to help it grow, and keep people where your customers need them most.

  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.
  • Industry observers note that microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S.
  • Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith mentioned the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

Industry observers note that microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith mentioned the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he noted most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which states it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

It has been revealed that his reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

Sources indicate that he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a recent development, his one example was an unnamed firm that wants to build in Finland. Google confirmed a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a massive technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

It has been revealed that rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

It has been revealed that smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate organization, and remarked Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

According to recent reports, smith noted Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

Sources indicate that he put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for challenges it considered important.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He noted the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he mentioned much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Smith mentioned the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

The second major trucking deal between Facebook parent firm Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 latest battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

In a recent development, “Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, noted Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”.

Industry observers note that meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This new Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The tech giant adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy newly introduced trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”.

Yuck. That's the feeling I get when reading this. Am I happy that more EV semi's will be going on the road? Yes. But the way it's being done just makes me feel dirty. And I refuse to do or have anything that Mark Zuckerberg is involved with. I find him to be disgusting. But then again I find most of these super wealthy people to be vomit inducing.

So I'd liken this deal to a guy who goes out to a bar with the sole intention of "having some fun". And it doesn't matter to him how that happens, as long as he gets his happy ending. But then when the sun rises and the darkness vanishes, who this guy slept with is revealed and it's not good.

Zucherberg isn't doing any of this for the planet. He's doing it for money.
