#157618. Industry News: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1187 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 fresh articles.
  • “Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes.
  • Sources indicate that I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 fresh articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last.

“Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work.

Sources indicate that I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom.

Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against the work it replaces.

In a recent development, at Bergens Tidende, known as BT, reporters publish 15 to 20 stories of their own a day. AI is not, for now, permitted to write them, but it does write a short version of the finished story, which the reporter is responsible for checking before an editor checks it too. Jan Stian Vold, BT’s development editor, estimates that a reporter who knows the story needs anything from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and that the editor’s look adds a minute or two. Writing the short version by hand, he told me, takes a reporter three to five minutes. These are his estimates, not measurements. Still, for the person who wrote the story, checking the machine’s version takes less time than writing one.

Vold’s guess is that about one short version in ten needs a fix, and he notes the summaries have kept improving with the models. The usual problem is clumsy grammar, or a summary that misses what the reporter considers the most vital point. “Almost never hallucinations,” he wrote to me. As far as BT knows, it has never published a critical mistake this way.

It has been revealed that office workers describe something different. In a Workday survey of 3,200 employees who use AI at large companies, nearly 40% of the time AI saved was lost to rework. In a survey of 1,150 U.S. employees by researchers at BetterUp and Stanford, each piece of workslop, AI-generated work that looks finished and is not, took nearly two hours to deal with. These are self-reports about longer documents, not a like-for-like comparison with a newsroom summary. But one difference stands out. In the office, the check often falls to someone who did not do the work and first has to find out what a right answer would look like. At BT, it falls to the one person who already knows.

Sources indicate that A Georgia Tech researcher argued this month that catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden that eats the gains. In the one newsroom where I could estimate it, the check took less time than the writing it replaced, and the reason is who does the checking.

In a recent development, johanna Johansson, who works in AI Foundations at Schibsted Media, told me that “hallucinations are surprisingly common.” Vold had written “almost never.” Both can be right. She was speaking of AI-generated content in general, he of one narrow task, the summary of a text the reporter has just finished. Two things may be at work here, and I cannot separate them: a narrow task may produce fewer errors, and a checker who knows the material may spot the ones that remain faster.

Industry observers note that on one point they agree. “Generally we always have a human in the loop,” Johansson remarked. That was always a firm principle, she said, and the huge improvements in the models have not made it any less important.

A judgment call, I would add, is the kind of error that only someone who knows the story is likely to notice.

In a recent development, so has the checking gone up or down? For BT’s newsroom as a whole, Vold could not say. His own work is administration and presentations, not journalism, and there his checking has gone down as he has learned to use AI as an assistant and not as a source of facts. At Fjell-Ljom it has stayed constant, because it was never a separate step. What nobody described is letting go of the check on what gets published.

I think they are right to hold that line, and the reason goes beyond the errors that remain. The check at BT is cheap because of everything the reporter did before the summary appeared. Hand the same summary to someone who had not reported the story, and the check would either take far longer or turn into a formality. A freelance journalist interviewed for a 2025 master’s thesis at Aalto University made a similar point: typing out an interview word for word “really gets you inside it in a way that reading over a transcription and just checking for errors doesn’t.”.

For companies outside the news business, I take three things from this. Count the check: how many items, how many people look at each one, and how many minutes each look takes. Then set that against what the task took before. Do not treat a falling error rate as permission to stop checking. Nobody I asked has. Above all, give the check to the person who knows the work, instead of adding a reviewer downstream who has to start from nothing. In these newsrooms, that is what keeps the check manageable.

As AI takes over more of what comes before the check, I would worry less about the minutes than about whether anyone is left who can tell in seconds that something is wrong.

“I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making big decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. Industry observers note that the actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative debuted this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

Industry observers note that at the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A new docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

And then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

In a recent development, the stakes are big. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

An analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common challenges, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching new customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

According to recent reports, “The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she said. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”.

2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she remarked.

According to recent reports, 3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

“Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she said.

It has been revealed that 4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

“You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she said. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”.

To see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the substantial-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.

Latest Update: From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary launched his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • According to recent reports, the Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary launched his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

According to recent reports, the Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The company recently shifted again, adding a newly introduced line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary noted, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

According to recent reports, high school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the complications.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

Sources indicate that when I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there swiftly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

That ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally crucial: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

Sources indicate that I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Newly introduced York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

In a recent development, AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

According to recent reports, nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

  • LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting fresh gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The fresh S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

The other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

Recent findings suggest that GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

Sources indicate that there’s an key caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T claims it is at the moment fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a manufacturer to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

Recent findings suggest that the analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The organization has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

According to recent reports, I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

It has been revealed that now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The tech giant indicated off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The tech giant also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

It has been revealed that both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The fresh models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha revealed off its newly introduced NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s new compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway showed off a newly introduced vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The latest Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

According to recent reports, NIU showed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company showed off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push newly introduced tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the firm has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

Sources indicate that with its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no unveiled production prepares, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Recent findings suggest that vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A latest Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

Fake Black Friday deals: where the savings come from framing

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fake Black Friday deals can look like bargains while saving less than promised, from inflated original prices to add-on warranties, padded bundles and minimum-spend shipping.
  • Sources indicate that A discount isn't a price.
  • Recent findings suggest that black Friday lets retailers play that game at scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fake Black Friday deals can look like bargains while saving less than promised, from inflated original prices to add-on warranties, padded bundles and minimum-spend shipping.

Sources indicate that A discount isn't a price. It's a comparison. A sale tag only means something next to a reference number, and the retailer usually gets to pick that number. It might be a list price, a "compare at" figure or a price the item carried for a few days back in October. Swap the reference and the same checkout total can pass for a small markdown or a steep one.

Recent findings suggest that black Friday lets retailers play that game at scale. The day itself falls after U.S. Thanksgiving, which is the fourth Thursday of November, but it stopped being a single day years ago. Promotions now run for weeks, online and in stores, and "early Black Friday" sales often start well before the date.

Industry observers note that A fake Black Friday deal is one where the savings come from how the price is presented, not from the price itself. Some lean on a reference price the product almost never sold at. Others push scarcity, swap in a cheaper version of a familiar product or pad the offer with add-ons that aren't worth much. A few just move the cost somewhere else: a monthly installment, a protection blueprint, a shipping minimum.

Sources indicate that the Federal Trade Commission has rules against deceptive former-price claims in the U.S. Shoppers don't have to rely on enforcement, though. Price-history trackers, model numbers and the fine print on a promotion usually reveal what a discount is actually worth.

Recent findings suggest that the 10 practices below aren't ranked. Each one is a different way a Black Friday price tag can overpromise, covering price framing, limited stock, lower-spec products, bundles, extended warranties, gift card offers, buy-now-pay-later aims, prices that were already low, last-generation electronics and minimum-spend shipping. For each, we explain how it works, how to spot it and what it can cost you.

Recent findings suggest that plenty of Black Friday discounts are real, and some are big. The point is to tell the difference between a deal that lowers what you pay and one that just dresses up the same price.

It has been revealed that A Black Friday discount is only as real as the original price it is measured against. When the crossed-out figure is set high, or the item rarely sold at it, a large percentage off can describe a modest saving or none at all.

This comparison is known as reference pricing. The struck-through number beside a sale price is the reference point a shopper uses to judge the offer. It might be a list price, a manufacturer's suggested retail price or a regular price from the store's own records.

Those labels do not mean the same thing. The manufacturer's suggested retail price, or MSRP, is a recommendation from the brand. Many products sell below it for much of their time on the market. A discount measured against MSRP can look generous while matching what other stores charge in an ordinary week.

Phrases such as "compare at" and "valued at" work in a similar way. They point to a price at another seller, or to a notional value, rather than a price the shopper would have paid at that store. The tag does not say which seller charged that amount, when it did so or whether anyone bought at it.

Industry observers note that the U.S. Federal Trade Commission publishes guidance on former-price comparisons. Its general principle is that an advertised reduction should start from a price the seller genuinely offered. A claim printed on a price tag is still not proof that the original price was real.

Shoppers can check a reference price with price-history tools. Camelcamelcamel and Keepa track prices on Amazon $AMZN listings and display them as charts. A chart indicates whether the higher price held for months or appeared only briefly. Both services also offer browser extensions and price-drop alerts.

Industry observers note that for items sold outside Amazon, a useful test is the current price of the identical model at several other retailers. If competitors list the same product near the advertised sale price, the percentage off mostly reflects the tag one store chose to display.

The number that decides whether an offer is a bargain is the final price paid, not the size of the markdown. A price below what other sellers charge is a saving whatever percentage appears beside it. A steep percentage off a price few people paid is a framing choice rather than a lower cost.

Industry observers note that A doorbuster is a heavily advertised price that a retailer may stock in very small quantities. Its main job is to bring shoppers into the store or onto the site, where they may buy other items at regular prices.

In a recent development, the strategy behind it is the loss leader. A store accepts a thin margin, or even a loss, on one featured product. It expects to make that back on everything else in the basket. A discounted television can draw in a shopper who then picks up a soundbar, cables, a wall mount and a few unrelated gifts. The advertised price does its work whether or not that shopper ever gets the television.

The limits usually sit in the fine print of the circular or the product page. Phrases such as "while supplies last," "limited quantities" and "no rain checks" signal that the store has made no promise to meet demand. Some ads state a minimum number of units per location. A minimum tells shoppers the store will carry at least that many. It says nothing about how many people will be waiting for them.

According to recent reports, timing adds another restriction. Many doorbusters apply only during a set window, such as the first hours after a store opens or a scheduled online release. Once that window closes or the stock runs out, the same shelf may hold a similar product at a higher price.

That substitution is where the real cost shows up. A shopper who planned a trip around one price may buy the nearest alternative rather than leave empty-handed. The alternative may be a different brand, a larger size or a model that was never discounted at all.

It has been revealed that before going after a doorbuster, read the quantity and time wording in the ad. Decide in advance what to buy, if anything, if the item sells out. Look up the regular price of a fallback model at other retailers. That reference makes it easier to judge whether the in-store substitute is a real deal or simply the next product on the shelf.

It has been revealed that some TVs, laptops, and other electronics sold for Black Friday are built specifically for the holiday sales rush. They often resemble a brand's regular models but use cheaper components. The low price can reflect a lesser product rather than a real markdown.

These products are sometimes called derivative models. A manufacturer produces a variant of an existing design for a particular retailer or sales event. The outer shell, the brand name and much of the marketing copy can match the familiar version. The differences tend to sit inside.

According to recent reports, in TVs, the cuts can show up in the panel and the connections. A made-for-sale set may have fewer HDMI ports, a lower refresh rate or a dimmer, simpler display panel. It may lack features such as local dimming that appear on similar-looking sets from the same brand. Those gaps matter most to buyers who play video games, watch in bright rooms or plan to connect several devices.

In a recent development, laptops follow a similar pattern. A holiday version may ship with less memory, a smaller or slower storage drive, a lower-tier processor or a lower-resolution screen. The chassis may use more plastic, and battery capacity can differ. Less memory and storage leave less headroom as software becomes more demanding over the years a laptop is kept.

Sources indicate that one common warning sign is an unfamiliar model number. A product that appears at only one retailer, or only during the sales season, may have no regular-price history to compare against. That makes any "was" price hard to judge. It also means reviews of a brand's mainstream model may not describe the product on the shelf.

A shopper can check by copying the exact model number from the listing. The next step is searching for it on the manufacturer's own website and reading the full specification sheet. Comparing that sheet line by line with the brand's standard model in the same size or range shows where the parts differ. A model number that returns no manufacturer page at all is itself useful information.

A made-for-sale product is not automatically a poor buy. A cheaper TV with fewer ports can work in a spare bedroom where only one device is connected. The relevant question is whether the price is low for the product actually in the box, not for the better model it resembles.

A Black Friday bundle saves money only if the shopper would have bought every item in it anyway. When the package includes extras with little use or resale value, the real discount on the main product can shrink to very little.

Retailers and manufacturers build bundles by pairing a headline product with add-ons. A game console might come with a game or a second controller. A camera might ship with a memory card, a bag and a basic tripod. A laptop might include a software subscription, a sleeve or a wireless mouse.

Recent findings suggest that the advertised bundle value is often the sum of each component's individual list price. That figure can look large on a sign or a product page. It does not show what the shopper would actually pay for those items separately, or whether the shopper wants them at all.

In a recent development, low-cost accessories are common padding. Cases, screen protectors, charging cables and generic earbuds are widely sold at low prices outside of any sale. Counting them at full list price inflates the stated value of the package.

Bundled games and software need a separate look. A console bundle may include a title the buyer has no interest in, or a download code for an older release. A software subscription may cover only a trial period. Some trials renew at full price unless the buyer cancels.

In a recent development, bundles also make prices harder to compare. A single product has one price that a shopper can check against other stores. A package of four or five items has no direct equivalent elsewhere. That hides the effective price of the main item.

The practical check is to price the core product on its own at several retailers. Then add only the accessories the buyer would have purchased regardless, at their usual selling prices. If that total is close to or below the bundle price, the bundle offers little extra.

Return terms are worth reading before checkout. Policies for bundles vary by retailer. Some stores may require the entire package back, including every opened accessory, rather than accepting a single item.

Recent findings suggest that A bundle can still be a reasonable purchase. When every piece fills a real need, buying them together can save time and sometimes money. The test is whether the savings hold up once the unwanted extras are set aside.

An extended warranty or protection proposal sold at checkout often covers problems the shopper is already protected against. Its price can also cancel out much of the discount that made the item look like a bargain.

Most newly introduced electronics and appliances come with a manufacturer's warranty. That coverage typically handles defects in materials and workmanship for a set period at no extra cost. A protection blueprint bought on the same day usually runs alongside it. The early months of paid coverage can duplicate what the manufacturer already provides.

Legal protections add another layer. In the U.S., most states recognize an implied warranty of merchantability, which requires that a product work for its ordinary purpose. Sellers can disclaim it in some states, so the terms of sale matter. In the U.K., the Consumer Rights Act 2015 gives buyers rights to a repair, replacement or refund when goods are faulty. Neither protection requires paying for a separate proposal.

Recent findings suggest that some credit cards also extend the manufacturer's warranty on purchases made with the card. These benefits vary by issuer and by card, and some issuers have reduced or dropped them. A shopper can check the current benefits guide for a specific card before assuming the coverage exists.

Industry observers note that the terms of a paid plan set its real value. Many plans exclude accidental damage unless it is listed. They also commonly exclude cosmetic damage, normal wear and misuse. Plans that do cover accidental damage may charge a deductible or service fee for each claim.

According to recent reports, the claims process matters as much as the coverage. Some intends require the owner to ship the device away for repair, leaving them without it for a period. Others may replace a failed product with a refurbished unit rather than a fresh one. Plans are often run by a third-party administrator rather than by the store itself.

Timing is part of the pitch. A protection plan offered at the register arrives when a shopper has already committed to the purchase and has little time to compare options. Some retailers and manufacturers let buyers add coverage for a period after the sale. The decision does not always have to be made at the counter.

The math takes one step. Subtract the cost of the plan from the advertised saving. The remaining figure is the real discount on the purchase.

A spend-and-get gift card promotion does not lower the price a shopper pays at the register. The bonus card has value only if the shopper returns to the same retailer, spends it before any deadline and follows its terms.

These Black Friday offers usually follow a simple pattern. A shopper buys a qualifying item or spends past a set amount, and the store hands over a gift card or store credit. The receipt still demonstrates the full sale price. The reward sits on a card that works only at that chain.

Recent findings suggest that that difference matters when comparing two offers. A direct discount leaves money in a shopper's pocket at checkout. A gift card with the same face value keeps that money inside the retailer's own system. The shopper must make a second purchase to collect any benefit at all.

Recent findings suggest that that second purchase often costs more than the card covers. A gift card rarely matches the exact price of the next item a shopper wants. The shopper pays the difference out of pocket. That extra spending also goes to the same retailer.

Promotional cards can also carry tighter rules than gift cards bought with cash, including earlier expiration dates. Some bonus cards work only during a set redemption window, which may not open until well after the original purchase. Others exclude certain brands, categories or items already on sale.

Industry observers note that returns add another complication. A retailer may reduce the refund on a returned item by the value of the bonus card, or ask for the unused card back. A shopper can check the return policy before buying rather than after.

Recent findings suggest that any balance left unspent stays with the retailer. The industry term for gift card value that never gets redeemed is breakage. That unredeemed value counts in the store's favor, not the shopper's.

Before picking a gift card offer over a cash discount elsewhere, a shopper can weigh three questions. Would they shop at this store again soon anyway? Can they meet the redemption dates? Does the fine print exclude what they plan to buy next?

Splitting a Black Friday purchase into installments through Klarna, Affirm or Afterpay changes when a shopper pays, not how much. A pay-later blueprint spreads a cost over time. It is not a discount, and in some cases it raises the total a shopper pays.

Retailers often display installment options right next to the sale price. A product listing or checkout page may show a small per-payment figure in large type. The full price may appear nearby in smaller print. That framing can make an expensive television or laptop look cheaper than it is. The total owed stays the same, or grows.

In a recent development, many short-term plans split a purchase into a handful of equal payments over several weeks. Some of these charge no interest when every payment arrives on time. Longer plans for larger purchases work more like a conventional loan. Some of them charge interest, and the rate depends on the lender, the plan and the borrower.

Missed payments carry their own costs. Depending on the provider and the proposal, a late payment can bring a fee. Some lenders also run credit checks or report payment history to credit bureaus. A shopper should read the specific terms before agreeing, rather than assume every pay-later plan works the same way.

Stacking plans is a separate risk. Each plan can look manageable on its own. Several plans opened at different stores over one shopping weekend can overlap, though. Those payments may come due in the same weeks and draw on the same bank account or card. One provider's app does not show plans held with other lenders, so the shopper has to track the combined total.

It has been revealed that returns add another step. A refund has to move through the lender as well as the retailer. A shopper who sends an item back should confirm with the provider whether scheduled payments pause while the return is processed.

Recent findings suggest that one check cuts through the framing. Add up the total paid under the proposal and compare it with the upfront price. If the plan adds fees or interest, the Black Friday discount shrinks by that amount. An installment schedule changes the timing of the payments, not what the item costs.

According to recent reports, A Black Friday price is not always a new low. Many advertised Black Friday prices match what the same product cost earlier in the fall. The November tag can simply repeat an earlier offer.

Retailers often attach the Black Friday name to promotions that start early in November. When the same discount carries through to the Friday itself, the date adds a label rather than a lower price. An item at its holiday price in the first week of the month can sit at that figure until the weekend.

Sources indicate that other sales events can set an equal or lower mark. Amazon $AMZN's Prime Day, back-to-school promotions and Labor Day sales in the U.S. all cut prices on electronics, appliances and home goods. A price reached at one of those events can match or beat the Black Friday offer on the same item.

According to recent reports, A price-history chart shows whether the Black Friday figure has appeared before. For products sold on Amazon, Camelcamelcamel and Keepa chart how a listing's price has moved over time. If the same figure shows up several times earlier in the year, it is a recurring price, not a one-time cut.

It has been revealed that this check answers a different question from whether a store's "was" price is genuine. A product can have an honest original price and still hit its holiday sale price several times a year. The useful comparison is with the lowest recent price, not the list price printed beside the discount.

Store policies can also reduce the pressure to buy on a single day. Some retailers match a competitor's lower price. Some refund the difference if their own price drops within a set period after purchase. Terms differ from store to store, and holiday periods can carry separate rules. The current policy is worth reading before checkout.

Prices can shift again after the Friday. Cyber Monday, the Monday after Thanksgiving, brings another round of online discounts. December sales can bring others.

A repeated price is not a bad price. It does mean the Black Friday date adds little urgency. A shopper who misses it may see the same figure at the next major sale event.

Steep Black Friday markdowns on phones, laptops, tablets and game consoles often apply to models that have already been replaced or are about to be. The price cut reflects the product's age in its release cycle, not a one-off act of generosity from the retailer.

Sources indicate that electronics makers refresh many product lines on a fairly regular schedule. Apple $AAPL has introduced most of its new iPhone lineups at events in September. That leaves the previous year's models on shelves in November, beside newer versions that launched only weeks earlier.

It has been revealed that retailers and carriers have a reason to clear older inventory before the holiday shopping season ends. A Black Friday promotion is one way to move it.

According to recent reports, the listing may not spell any of this out. A product page can describe an item as fresh, which is accurate in the sense that it is unopened and unused. That word indicates nothing about when the model first went on sale. A shopper who sees a large discount on a laptop may not realize its processor belongs to a chip generation that has since been superseded.

It has been revealed that A few checks can establish a model's age. The manufacturer's website usually lists the current lineup, and a model missing from it has likely been discontinued. Product reviews and manufacturers' press pages give the date a model first went on sale.

Recent findings suggest that the trade-offs go beyond raw speed. Phones and tablets depend on software updates for security fixes and new features. Every device eventually stops receiving those updates. An older model reaches that cutoff sooner than a newer one bought on the same day.

Many manufacturers publish revision policies for their recent devices, and those pages show how long support is promised. Older hardware may also lack newer ports, wireless standards or camera features that later models added.

A last-generation device can still suit a buyer who wants a capable phone or laptop at a lower price and does not need the newest features. The useful comparison is between the discounted older model and the current one. That means weighing the gap in price against the gap in specs and the years of software support each has left.

A free shipping offer that applies only above a minimum order total can cost more than it saves. If reaching the threshold means adding items a shopper did not blueprint to buy, the extra spending can exceed the delivery fee it was meant to avoid.

The mechanics are straightforward. A retailer sets an order value at which shipping charges drop away. A shopper whose cart sits just below that line faces a choice. They can pay for delivery, or they can add something to cross the line. The threshold works for the retailer when shoppers take the second path.

It has been revealed that the added item is the part to examine. Online stores often show low-cost products near the cart or checkout page, such as socks, phone chargers, batteries or small household goods. These fillers make it easy to close the gap. Whether that counts as a saving depends on whether the shopper needed the item.

It has been revealed that A quick comparison settles the question. Set the shipping fee against the price of the filler item. If the filler costs more than the fee and serves no real need, paying for delivery is the cheaper outcome. If the filler was already on the shopping list, crossing the threshold can make sense.

Several alternatives can remove the threshold from the decision. Many large chains let shoppers buy online and pick up in store, generally without a delivery charge. Some retailers sell paid memberships that include free shipping without an order minimum. That membership fee pays off only for shoppers who order often enough to offset it. A retailer's threshold during a holiday promotion may also differ from its usual one.

Returns deserve a look before checkout. Free outbound shipping does not guarantee free return shipping. Some retailers deduct a return shipping fee or a restocking charge from refunds. Those policies can vary by product category. A filler item that ends up being sent back may cost the shopper money twice.

It has been revealed that the threshold itself is a pricing tool rather than a discount. It encourages larger orders. Each delivery then carries more merchandise, which spreads the retailer's shipping cost across a bigger sale.

Europe’s first spot Bitcoin ETF debuted with 350 BTC worth more than $20 million, opening a new chapter for the country’s regulated crypto investment market. BIT Asset Management’s Bitcoin Fund ETF (BBIT) began trading on the SIX Swiss Exchange yesterday with Bitcoin exposure through a Swiss fund structure.

BBIT itself carries an annual expense ratio of 0.19% and is currently Europe’s only active spot Bitcoin ETF.

Recent findings suggest that 🇨🇭 Today, Bitcoin Fund ETF (BBIT) will list on SIX Swiss Exchange: Switzerland’s first and only FINMA-approved Bitcoin ETF.🕘 Trading opens at 9:00 CET (8:00 UTC)News announcement: https://t.co/N112jUZiUP*Switzerland only. Not for US persons. Capital at risk. pic.twitter.com/CJa7lkh3uT.

Recent findings suggest that the launch followed an 18-month regulatory process, with FINMA approving the fund on October 20. The approval then allows BBIT to invest exclusively in Bitcoin under a specific exemption from diversification requirements, opening a route for investors whose mandates restrict them to fund-based investments.

“Some institutional investors may face internal investment restrictions that permit investments only through fund structures,” Dominik Oggenfuss, CEO of BIT Asset Management, told Cryptonews in an exclusive comment.

It has been revealed that switzerland already has an established market for Bitcoin investment products, but not every investor can use every available vehicle. Some institutional mandates permit investments in funds while restricting exchange-traded notes or other product structures, creating a compliance barrier even when Bitcoin exposure is otherwise allowed.

Recent findings suggest that BBIT addresses these differences through its Swiss fund structure, operating under Swiss fund law and FINMA oversight. Rather than relying on futures contracts or gaining Bitcoin exposure through an issuer’s debt, BBIT fund holds Bitcoin directly.

According to recent reports, its holdings are stored in cold storage through AMINA Bank under Swiss banking regulation, offering institutions a custody arrangement within Switzerland’s financial system. Investors can buy fund shares through participating banks and brokers on SIX, using existing investment infrastructure, bypassing the hassles of managing wallets or/and private keys.

Oggenfuss said the fund was designed for investors who already had Bitcoin exposure but wanted a different regulatory and custody arrangement.

“Some investors already had access to Bitcoin through ETPs but would prefer a Swiss fund structure under Swiss Fund Law, regulated by FINMA, combined with a Swiss cold-storage solution provided by AMINA Bank under Swiss banking regulation,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that this structure could make a difference for institutions operating under strict investment policies. These restrictions dictate eligible asset classes, legal structures, custody arrangements and counterparties, so a upcoming investment vehicle can open access even when the underlying asset is already available elsewhere.

BBIT also offers Bitcoin-in-kind subscriptions, allowing eligible investors to contribute Bitcoin directly to the fund. Combined with its 0.19% expense ratio, the fund is positioning itself at the center of institutional infrastructure, cost, and operational convenience.

“BIT Group is not a firm that discovered Bitcoin recently. From one of the first Satoshi White Paper translations to a Swiss Bitcoin ETF, that continuity is a story many competitors cannot tell,” Oggenfuss noted.

BIT is presenting BBIT as the culmination of a much longer involvement with Bitcoin. Switzerland’s exchange market has been building crypto investment infrastructure for nearly a decade. SIX introduced Bitcoin-linked structured products in 2016, followed by physically backed crypto investment products as the market expanded.

It has been revealed that the growth of these products has expanded access to Bitcoin through regulated exchanges, but fund mandates continued to dictate which structures institutions could use. BBIT introduces another option within this existing ecosystem, placing direct Bitcoin holdings inside a Swiss fund framework.

BBIT’s 350 Bitcoin launch gives the ETF a starting base of more than $20 million as BIT looks to attract investors through Swiss banking and brokerage networks. Now, we will see if this can turn regulatory approval and structural flexibility into sustained inflows.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

The hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts noted last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, indicates that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

Sources indicate that according to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

Sources indicate that the green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

Sources indicate that the Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

Since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

It has been revealed that the Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

Goldman also mentioned that retail investors have been buying significant tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

According to recent reports, the Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

In the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief executive of one of the world’s leading fashion brands has said that the intense and often slow process of craftswomen and men making products by hand has become a vital skill in a world of online “instant gratification.”.

Leena Nair, the CEO of Chanel, noted that business leaders are living through an “unprecedented” period of transformation and fragility, adding that it was time to prioritize human ingenuity and talent.

“Macro-economic shifts, huge leaps in AI and technology and geopolitical instability, these are challenges affecting all sectors,” she told the annual gala dinner of the French Chamber of Great Britain, which brings together U.K. and French business executives, policy makers, and cultural leaders.

According to recent reports, “And in this context of disruption, the power of creation and beauty has never been more vital or more precious. Creation and beauty have been vital sources of inspiration and joy for thousands of years. They’re even more precious today in a world of constant instant gratification, constant overstimulation, and infinite touch points.”.

Nair, who has been Chanel CEO since 2022, saw the luxury brand return to growth last year, led by an increase in sales in America. Global revenues rose by 1.8% compared with 2024 to $19.3 billion, while operating profits rose 5.2% to $4.7 billion.

Nair said there was a growing body of scientific evidence that revealed that exposure to art and human-led creative work led to higher levels of happiness and performance.

“This growing body of academic research indicates how encounters with beauty correlate directly to a greater sense of human flourishing at work and in life,” she noted. “In recent years, we see growing scientific evidence of the improving impact that arts and culture has on physical and mental well-being.”.

“In this context of disruption, the power of creation and beauty has never been more vital or more precious”.

Over 95% of Chanel’s customers are women, Nair noted, adding that “beauty” is a very important driver of how people respond to the world around them. She said that one customer who had been through surgery said that buying crafted products was part of her recovery.

“Surgeons tell me this all the time, that when surgery is over they know the women are back to normal when they ask to put on their makeup for the first time,” she stated.

Recent findings suggest that many leaders of luxury brands often feel ignored when it comes to policy debates about economic growth. In the U.K., the end of foreign visitors being able to shop without incurring the national sales tax has caused controversy. In the U.S., latest tariffs targeting luxury goods have unsettled markets.

Sources indicate that “Luxury is an economic powerhouse, it’s a cultural powerhouse and an emotional powerhouse,” Nair stated. “To put that scale into context, European high-end luxury brands generate a trillion dollars in business every year. That’s 5% of Europe’s GDP. “It’s not a niche sector. More than 2 million people work in the sector across Europe.”.

Chanel works with the King’s Foundation, King Charles III’s organization that supports the retention and development of traditional skills.

“It looks simple, but to do a pleated skirt takes eight hours of pushing a cardboard mold back and forth by two talented artisans doing it the right way,” Nair mentioned, arguing that Chanel continues to invest in “skills that will otherwise be lost, working with extraordinary artisans and partners, many of whom we have worked with for generations.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • Sources indicate that amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Sources indicate that amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

The deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled prepares to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy noted on the company’s earnings call last month.

Amazon revealed the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

It has been revealed that decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” stated Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

It has been revealed that amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

It has been revealed that amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon stated last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other major buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

“From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf stated in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

According to recent reports, the deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large organization had finished moving a group of business customers onto a fresh billing platform. The implementation team completed migration testing, reconciled the account data and handed the platform to billing operations, which would run the process day to day.

It has been revealed that operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

According to recent reports, three weeks later, billing specialists began finding a recurring problem in a small set of migrated accounts. The records matched the approved migration rules, but certain combinations of account settings forced specialists to correct fields manually before an invoice could be released.

Each correction was manageable, but the pattern became expensive only after the same work kept appearing in normal billing activity.

The difference became clearer at the next billing cycle.

It has been revealed that the affected accounts didn’t fail in the same way every time. One required a manual tax treatment, another needed a contract setting corrected, and another triggered an exception only after a billing adjustment.

Each case looked like “ordinary operating cleanup” until the team compared them and found the migration pattern underneath. That comparison took time because the work was being recorded where it occurred.

None of those activities were recorded as a reopened implementation problem while the project remained closed.

In a recent development, the cost highlighted up first in operating time. Billing specialists who should have been reviewing current invoices were opening migrated accounts, comparing settings and correcting fields before invoices could move.

Sources indicate that team leads added exception checks to the billing cycle, and finance partners joined troubleshooting calls to understand why the same account pattern kept reappearing. Customer-service teams then had to answer questions when invoice timing slipped for affected accounts.

It has been revealed that the extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

According to recent reports, the billing team also had to protect normal work while dealing with the exceptions. Meanwhile, experienced specialists spent part of each cycle correcting migrated accounts, which left less time for current billing issues that had nothing to do with the migration.

As the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

This is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

According to recent reports, those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

Once the project closed, the operating cost had no direct route back into the measure that had already recorded the implementation as complete. The consequence stayed visible, but it lived in a different record.

The sensible response was to strengthen acceptance before the next group of customers. The company did three things:.

Recent findings suggest that those changes helped. More configuration problems were caught before transfer, and operations had a stronger basis for accepting the work.

Industry observers note that the acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

In a recent development, for the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration concerns before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

A different pattern surfaced later.

A subset of accounts required manual correction only after a billing adjustment changed how two fields interacted. The migration had passed the stronger acceptance test because the concern didn’t appear until those accounts went through live billing activity.

It has been revealed that billing specialists again became the first people to see the consequence. They reopened affected accounts, compared the upcoming exceptions with the earlier corrections and traced which cases required manual handling before invoices could move.

The implementation record still showed a “completed migration” while the added work accumulated inside the billing cycle.

In a recent development, the company also kept the implementation team available during a stabilization period. That gave operations a route back when the account pattern became clear.

Industry observers note that support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

It has been revealed that the technical matter was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

According to recent reports, A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

A pattern like this becomes especially hard to see when both records are accurate. An implementation team can show that the agreed migration work passed its tests and was accepted. Operations can show that the live process now requires additional effort.

No one has to misreport anything. The separation sits in where each result is counted.

That’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.
