It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Recent findings suggest that hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the latest Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

Industry observers note that hyundai noted the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car).

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

Industry observers note that most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the new Kona’s wheel design.

It has been revealed that while earlier reports suggested Hyundai planned to drop the all-electric Kona variant and would only offer gas and hybrid versions, the prototype captured in Korea is expected to be the EV model. However, Hyundai has yet to confirm powertrain or battery specs.

The updates are even more evident on the inside. Previous spy images appeared to show the third-gen Hyundai Kona running Hyundai’s upcoming Pleos Connect infotainment system, like the IONIQ 3.

In the IONIQ 3, Hyundai offers a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Like the current model, the third-gen Kona is expected to be available with fully electric (EV), hybrid, and gas-powered powertrains.

While Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona EV, the electric version could return in 2027 or 2028 when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

The hybrid version will likely use the same 1.6L hybrid engine as the newly introduced Seltos, while the EV variant could offer similar powertrain and battery options to the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 3 is available with two battery packs in Europe and the UK: 42 kWh and 61 kWh, offering WLTP ranges of up to 213 miles (344 km) and 308 miles (497 km), respectively.

#157606. Small Business Saturday: 10 ways to shop local this Black Friday weekend

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4121 w)
📖 Baca

Small Business Saturday: 10 ways to shop local this Black Friday weekend

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These 10 ways to shop local on Small Business Saturday, from gift cards and independent bookstores to reviews and makers' markets, explain how each one helps a neighborhood business.
  • In a recent development, where you buy a holiday gift decides how much of the money stays with the business that sold it.
  • Small Business Saturday sits right in the middle of that math.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These 10 ways to shop local on Small Business Saturday, from gift cards and independent bookstores to reviews and makers' markets, explain how each one helps a neighborhood business.

In a recent development, where you buy a holiday gift decides how much of the money stays with the business that sold it. A sale on a significant online marketplace comes with a commission the seller pays. A card payment comes with a processing fee the merchant absorbs. A gift card bought in November puts cash in a shop's register before the recipient ever walks through the door. None of that shows up on a receipt, but all of it affects what an independent owner actually keeps.

Small Business Saturday sits right in the middle of that math. It falls on the Saturday after Thanksgiving, wedged between Black Friday and Cyber Monday. American Express $AXP started it in 2010 to carve out one day for independent businesses in a weekend that otherwise belongs to substantial-box chains and online deals. Independent shops, restaurants and service businesses now proposal sales and events around it.

In a recent development, for shoppers, the useful question is a practical one. Showing up matters, but some ways of spending leave more money with a local business than others. And several of the most helpful things you can do are free. A detailed review can help a shop turn up in map and search results. A word to a friend can bring in a customer the shop never had to pay to reach.

In a recent development, the 10 ideas below cover both kinds of support. Some involve buying: gift cards, books from an independent bookstore, orders placed through a shop's own website, food from local kitchens, classes given as gifts and finds from farmers markets and makers' markets. Others are about how you pay, what you post online and who you tell. One looks past the weekend altogether, since independent businesses depend on sales that keep coming through December and into the fresh year.

Each one works on its own. None takes a big budget, and none guarantees a particular payoff for the business. Together, they're a handful of practical ways to point your holiday spending toward the shops, bookstores, bakeries and studios in your own neighborhood.

A gift card from an independent shop puts money in the owner's hands at the moment of sale. The merchandise stays on the shelf until the card is redeemed, and the recipient gets to choose what they want.

In a recent development, that timing matters for a small retailer. Holiday inventory is usually ordered and paid for well before December. Cash that comes in on Small Business Saturday helps cover those costs, even though the goods it pays for may leave the store long after the sale.

In a recent development, gift cards also bring upcoming people through the door. A recipient who has never visited the shop now has a reason to walk in, browse and learn what it carries. Some recipients spend beyond the card's value. Others come back later on their own.

Most independent shops sell cards at the counter. Many also sell them through their own websites, often as digital cards delivered by email. A digital card suits a recipient who lives in another city or a gift that has to arrive on short notice. A physical card can go inside a holiday card or be wrapped with a small item from the same shop.

Read the terms before buying. In the U.S., the federal Credit CARD Act of 2009 bars most retail gift cards from expiring within five years. That clock runs from the purchase date or the last time money was loaded onto the card. State laws can add further protections. Ask whether the card works at every location if the business has more than one. Ask too whether it covers sale items, services or online orders.

A small business can close or change hands. Keeping the receipt helps if a card is lost or disputed. Registering a digital card, where the shop offers that option, does the same.

Industry observers note that the choice of shop can reflect the recipient. A card for a neighborhood hardware store, a toy shop or a record store points to their interests. It still leaves the final pick to them.

In a recent development, an independent bookstore can get almost any book in print, not only the titles on its shelves. Booksellers routinely take special orders for titles a customer requests. Many also ship books to a customer's home or straight to a gift recipient.

Special orders run through the same channels a store uses to restock. Bookstores buy from publishers and from book wholesalers. Either route can usually supply a title that is still in print. Giving the bookseller the ISBN, the 13-digit number printed near the barcode, removes confusion between editions, translations and formats.

A special order usually takes longer than buying a book off the shelf. That makes holiday timing something to initiative around. Publishers' warehouses and shipping carriers handle heavy volume in late November and December. Popular titles can also sell out before a reprint arrives. Placing gift orders during Black Friday weekend leaves room for those delays.

Preorders follow the same logic for books not yet published. A shop can reserve a forthcoming title for a customer. It can then set the copy aside or ship it when the stock comes in.

Staff recommendations are one advantage of shopping in person. Booksellers spend their working days handling upcoming releases and older backlist titles. Describing the recipient helps. A favorite author, a recent book they enjoyed or a subject they follow gives a bookseller enough to suggest titles a search algorithm might not surface. Many stores mark staff picks with handwritten shelf cards.

Check a shop's event calendar in December. Independent bookstores host author readings, signings, children's story hours and book club meetings. Some sell signed copies after those events. A signed book can make a more personal gift than a standard copy.

It has been revealed that secondhand books are another option. Some independent shops sell used books alongside new ones. Dedicated used bookstores can carry out-of-print titles that a new-book shop has no way to order.

According to recent reports, ask about holiday services before checking out. Some shops offer gift wrapping. Others hold orders for in-store pickup or mail books to a recipient in another city.

Ordering from a local shop's own website, or calling the store, keeps the sale off large online marketplaces. Those platforms charge sellers a commission on each sale. A direct order leaves more of the purchase price with the business that made the sale.

According to recent reports, many independent retailers list products on major marketplaces to reach shoppers who would never find them otherwise. That reach comes at a cost. Marketplace sellers typically pay a cut of every order. Some platforms add charges for advertising, storage or fulfillment. The exact terms vary by platform and by product category.

A shop's own site works differently. The merchant still pays for web hosting and an online store platform. No marketplace takes a share of each order, though. Shops that don't sell online at all can often take an order by phone or email instead.

Finding the direct route is usually straightforward. A shop's web address often appears on its receipts, shopping bags, business cards and social media profiles. Searching the store's name along with its city can bring up the official site alongside any marketplace listings. When a product appears in both places, buying it on the shop's own site is the direct sale.

Industry observers note that A shop's own site may also carry stock that never reaches a marketplace. One-off pieces, small batches and items made by nearby producers sometimes appear only there.

Sources indicate that check for local pickup before checkout. Many small retailers let customers order online and collect in store. That spares the buyer a shipping charge and spares the shop from preparing a parcel. It also brings the buyer through the door, where other items on the shelves are in view.

Industry observers note that shipping from a small shop can cost more or take longer than shipping from a large retailer with its own logistics network. Ordering early in the holiday season leaves room for that. Some shops post holiday shipping cutoff dates on their sites.

Direct orders also change who holds the customer relationship. Marketplaces often limit how sellers can contact buyers. When a shopper buys from the store's site, the shop can follow up on the order and answer questions itself. Returns and exchanges then go through the shop rather than a platform. Reading the store's own return policy before paying avoids confusion later.

Industry observers note that following an independent shop's stated payment preference is one of the simplest ways to help it on Small Business Saturday. A shop that asks for cash or debit is often trying to manage what card acceptance costs the business.

Every card sale carries processing fees. The merchant pays them, not the shopper. Several parties share those fees, including the bank that issued the card, the card network and the company that processes the payment. Depending on the processor, the charges come out of each deposit or arrive as a periodic bill.

Industry observers note that card money also takes time to arrive. Card sales settle through the processor and land in a merchant's bank account after a delay. Cash is in the register the moment the sale ends. For a small retailer paying for holiday inventory or covering extra staff in a busy month, that timing can matter.

Preference is the operative word. Cash carries its own costs for a business. Someone has to count it, store it securely and take it to the bank. Some owners would rather skip that work and run a fully card-based or cashless counter. Paying cash at a shop that does not want it does not help the owner.

It has been revealed that the clearest guide is the shop itself. Look for a sign at the register or a note on the shop's website. Some small businesses post a cash discount. Others add a surcharge for credit cards. Rules on surcharging vary by state and by card network. Card network rules generally bar surcharges on debit cards, even where credit surcharges are allowed.

Cashless stores are not allowed everywhere. Massachusetts, Upcoming Jersey, New York City, Philadelphia and San Francisco are among the places that generally require retail stores to accept cash. Those rules are meant to protect shoppers who do not have bank accounts or cards.

Recent findings suggest that A short question at checkout works when no sign is posted. Asking which payment method the shop prefers takes a few seconds. It costs the shopper nothing extra, and it leaves the decision with the owner.

Industry observers note that planning ahead makes this easier. Withdrawing cash before a trip to a downtown shopping district helps when several smaller vendors are on the list. Some pop-up sellers work mostly in cash, and a shopper without it may have to walk away from a purchase.

A specific, honest online review helps a local business appear when nearby shoppers search, and it costs the reviewer nothing. A review that names what was bought and how the visit went gives other customers far more to go on than a star rating alone.

In a recent development, search engines and map apps treat reviews as one of several signals when deciding which nearby businesses to show. A shop with recent, detailed reviews gives those systems more information to work with. It also gives a stranger scrolling through results a concrete reason to walk in.

It has been revealed that the most useful reviews read like a short report. Name the product or service, such as a hand-thrown mug, a house-made hot sauce or a bike tune-up. Mention whether the item was in stock or ordered in, and how long the wait was. Describe what the staff did, whether that meant tracking down a size, wrapping a gift or suggesting an alternative. Those details answer the practical questions future customers tend to ask.

Timing shapes a review's value as well. A review posted soon after a Small Business Saturday visit captures details while they are fresh. A post that week adds a recent entry during a season when many shoppers are deciding where to spend. Photos of the storefront, the shelves or the purchase can add context that text cannot.

In a recent development, honesty keeps a review useful. A balanced account that notes a long line or limited parking alongside good service gives readers a fuller picture than unqualified praise. Many review platforms bar reviews written in exchange for discounts or free products. A review should reflect a real purchase or visit. Owners can often reply publicly, and a constructive note gives them something concrete to act on.

Many independent shops work with limited advertising budgets. For a shop like that, its search listing and the reviews attached to it can be one of the first things a new customer sees. Each customer who writes a few clear sentences adds directly to that public record.

Recent findings suggest that A short review takes only a few minutes. It can be written on a phone before leaving the parking lot or later that evening. It stays attached to the business listing long after the holiday weekend ends.

Farmers markets and holiday makers' markets let shoppers buy straight from the people who grow, cook or craft the goods on the table. With no wholesaler or retail middleman involved, the vendor sets the price and collects the sale directly, minus any stall fee the market charges.

Recent findings suggest that that direct link is the main difference from a store shelf. A farmer selling apples, winter squash or eggs at a market booth is often the same person who raised them. A potter, woodworker or soapmaker at a craft fair usually made the pieces on display and can explain how.

Holiday makers' markets tend to appear in late November and December. They are often held in school gyms, church halls, community centers, breweries and public squares. Many run for a single weekend or one evening. The window to shop them can be short.

Sources indicate that outdoor farmers markets also shift with the season. In colder parts of the U.S., some move indoors for winter and cut back to fewer market days. Others close until spring. A market's own website or social media page is usually the most reliable place to confirm dates, hours and location before going.

Shelf-stable goods make practical gifts from these markets. Honey, jams, maple syrup and dried herbs travel well and keep for weeks or longer. Candles, soap and ceramics hold up in shipping and storage. Fresh produce and baked goods are better suited to a host gift or a holiday meal.

Sources indicate that face-to-face buying also allows questions that a product listing rarely answers. Shoppers can ask what wood a cutting board is made of, how a glazed mug should be cleaned or whether a soap contains fragrance. Farmers can explain how a crop was grown and how to store it.

It has been revealed that many makers take commissions and custom orders, such as a personalized ornament or a piece in a specific color. These requests need lead time. Asking in late November or early December rather than the week before a holiday gives the maker room to finish the work.

It has been revealed that vendors at seasonal markets often have no permanent storefront. Picking up a business card or noting a maker's name makes it possible to find them again. Many also sell between markets by email, by phone or at other recurring events.

A local class or service works as a holiday gift that sends money to a nearby business owner instead of a distant warehouse. A pottery class, a haircut or a pass for a neighborhood fitness studio all fit this approach.

Service businesses sell time and skill rather than stocked inventory. That puts studios, salons and independent instructors outside the doorbuster discounts that dominate Black Friday weekend promotions. A gift of their time gives them a holiday sale that doesn't depend on a shelf of products.

According to recent reports, most of these businesses sell gifts in one of a few forms. A studio may offer a single-session certificate, a multi-class pack or a set membership period. Salons and barbershops often sell certificates for a named service, such as a cut or a color appointment. Some instructors sell seats in a specific workshop on a set date. A question at the front desk will show which formats a business offers.

Booking terms matter more for experiences than for physical goods. Classes fill up, and instructors keep limited schedules. Some sessions run only in certain months. Before buying, check whether the gift is tied to a date and how far ahead the recipient needs to book. Ask what happens if they need to reschedule. Expiration rules vary by business and by location. Confirm them at the time of purchase.

In a recent development, A gift that fits the recipient's interests is easier for them to use. A beginner wheel-throwing class suits someone who likes working with their hands. A cooking class can suit someone who hosts often. A massage, a tailoring appointment or a bike tune-up can suit someone who rarely books those services for themselves.

In a recent development, many of these businesses work in small groups or one-on-one sessions. That format gives the recipient direct time with an instructor, stylist or technician. It also introduces the recipient to a business they may return to on their own.

A gift for two is another option. Paired classes, such as a couples' cooking night or a two-person workshop, let the giver attend alongside the recipient. Some studios also sell private group sessions for families or friends. Those sessions can double as a shared holiday outing.

The same idea works for a recipient who lives in another city. Many studios and salons take gift orders by phone or online. A giver can buy a session at an independent business near the recipient's home rather than near their own.

Ordering pies, platters and party trays from a neighborhood bakery or restaurant moves holiday food spending to local kitchens. Order early, order directly and plan the pickup. Many small kitchens can only produce so much in a single week.

Catering follows a similar timeline. Restaurants that sell trays of appetizers, roasted meats or side dishes usually ask for a headcount and a pickup date in advance. Some ask for a deposit to hold the order. Calling with a rough guest count makes it easier for the kitchen to suggest portions and quantities.

According to recent reports, dietary questions are easier to sort out with a local kitchen than with a packaged product. Customers can ask what goes into a dish and how it is prepared. They can also ask whether it contains nuts, dairy or gluten. Some small bakeries make egg-free or dairy-free versions on request. Shared equipment can still mean cross-contact. Asking the kitchen directly is the reliable way to know.

Industry observers note that how an order is placed also matters. Calling the restaurant, ordering at the counter or using its own online ordering page keeps the sale off third-party delivery apps. A direct order also lets staff confirm details or flag a sold-out item before the event.

Pickup is the final step. Holiday pickup days tend to be crowded, and many shops assign time slots to keep lines moving. Arriving within the assigned window helps the kitchen hand off orders while the food is fresh. Asking for reheating instructions for hot dishes saves guesswork at home.

Sources indicate that the same approach works for more than one dinner. Office parties, Upcoming Year's gatherings and winter potlucks all call for platters, desserts and bread. Restaurants that do not advertise catering may still take a large takeout order if a customer asks a few days ahead.

Small Business Saturday lasts a single day, but local shops need customers for the rest of the holiday season and well into the newly introduced year. Spreading purchases across December and January gives independent businesses steadier sales than one busy weekend can.

In a recent development, the Saturday event puts independent retailers in the spotlight for one weekend. The weeks that follow still bring gift buying, holiday hosting and year-end errands.

It has been revealed that last-minute gifts are easier to find at a store close to home. National carriers publish holiday shipping cutoffs, and orders placed after those dates may not arrive before Christmas. A shop down the street already has its stock on the shelf. A shopper can walk in on Dec. 23 and leave with a gift in hand.

Industry observers note that local staff can also help with a late gift. They know what is in stock and can suggest an alternative when a planned item has sold out. Some independent shops also wrap gifts at the counter. That saves time in the final days before a holiday.

Sources indicate that january brings its own reasons to buy close to home. Exchanges and returns are simpler when the store is nearby and the owner can handle them in person. Post-holiday clearance sales help local shops move seasonal inventory. Cold-weather needs such as boots, coats, snow shovels and ice melt send people to hardware and clothing stores in many parts of the U.S.

The quieter stretch after the holidays matters for owners too. Foot traffic often drops once the gift season ends. Rent, payroll and utility bills keep arriving each month regardless. A purchase during a slow week adds revenue when fewer customers are coming through the door.

One version of this approach is a routine. Picking up coffee beans, a birthday card or a replacement hardware part from an independent shop turns occasional support into regular business. Those everyday errands happen in every month, not only in late November.

One practical rule is to check a local store before ordering something online. That habit carries the purpose of Small Business Saturday into the rest of the year.

Telling friends about a local shop, or sharing its posts online, points new customers toward an independent business at no cost to you. The recommendation comes from someone the listener already knows, which gives it weight with them.

In a recent development, independent shops rarely have the marketing budgets of national chains. At many of them, the owner or a single employee runs the shop's social media accounts alongside other work. Each share, tag or mention carries the shop's name to people outside its usual audience.

Recent findings suggest that specific recommendations give friends something to act on. Saying a shop "is great" offers little detail. Naming the hand-poured candles, the cheese counter or the employee who tracked down a hard-to-find gift tells a friend why to go. It also tells them what to ask for.

Social media makes this kind of referral easy to repeat. Posting a photo of a holiday purchase and tagging the shop's account lets followers click straight through to its profile. Resharing the shop's own posts spreads the details an owner most wants customers to see. Those posts often cover newly introduced stock, extended holiday hours or a Small Business Saturday event.

In a recent development, adding a location tag to a post connects it to the shop's address. That helps followers who live nearby figure out where to find it.

Private messages and group chats count, too. A friend stuck on a gift for a relative can get a quick text with a link to a shop that fits. That one message can send a customer the shop might not have reached otherwise.

Email newsletters offer another direct line. Signing up means hearing about sales, restocks and events straight from the shop. The news arrives without depending on what a social platform chooses to display. Forwarding a newsletter to a friend passes that information along.

Sources indicate that neighborhood groups and community forums are another outlet. Someone may ask for gift ideas or a place to find a particular item. Naming a local shop in reply puts it in front of a person already planning to buy.

In a recent development, some owners prefer that customers not photograph certain items, displays or staff. Asking before posting from inside a shop respects that preference.

Recent findings suggest that mark Hurd, who until last month was one of two CEOs leading the database software giant Oracle, passed away this morning at age 62, one month after telling employees in a letter that he was taking a leave of absence owing to health reasons. TechCrunch has more here.

According to recent reports, softBank Group is assembling a rescue financing proposal for WeWork that may value the office-sharing tech giant below $8 billion, according to Bloomberg. The newly introduced figure is a fraction of the $47 billion valuation the startup commanded as recently as January, and yet it *still* seems a little high when compared with its bigger, profitable, publicly traded rival IWG, whose valuation is roughy half that amount.

Fun fact: Amazon went public in 1997 with $16 million in revenue and a market cap of $438 million. #ThoseWereTheDays. Unless you can write a $1 million check, it’s almost impossible to get exposure to early stage tech. Enter EquityZen. EquityZen allows accredited investors to access proven pre-IPO tech firms like Impossible Foods, SpaceX, Stripe, Rivian Automotive and Epic Games through its pooled funds. Explore EquityZen’s secondary market today.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, states Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it states it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the manufacturer,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s notable that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Tech giant earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”).

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

ArsenalBio, a year-old, South San Francisco-based biotech outfit that hopes to improve the ability of T cell therapies to better fight a broader range of cancers, has raised $85 million in Series A funding. Investors include Westlake Village BioPartners, the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Kleiner Perkins, the University of California, San Francisco Foundation Investment Tech giant, Euclidean Capital and Osage Venture Partners. TechCrunch has much more here.

Madbox, a 4.5-year-old, France-based mobile games studio, has raised $16.5 million in Series A funding from Alven. TechCrunch has more here.

Tenfold, a four-year-old, Austin, Tex.-based maker of customer service software, has raised $7.5 million in Series C funding led by Next Coast Ventures, with participation from earlier backers Andreessen Horowitz, Geekdom Fund, and Salesforce Ventures. Pulse 2.0 has more here.

Bloomberg Beta, the six-year-old, San Francisco-based outfit that uses Bloomberg LP’s money to make bets on startups, has closed its third fund with $75 million, according to Roy Bahat, who’d previously run the online media company IGN and who operates the fund as an equal partnership with Karin Klein and James Chan. (Klein formerly ran Bloomberg’s newly introduced initiatives; Chan was formerly a principal with Trinity Ventures.) We talked with Bahat briefly last night about the new vehicle to ask how its capital will be deployed.

Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1251 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • It has been revealed that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app reveals the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

It has been revealed that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

Sources indicate that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

Recent findings suggest that for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

It has been revealed that the SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Sources indicate that under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks indicates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

In a recent development, the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

Recent findings suggest that the SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Sources indicate that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

Tech Report: 5 trends that will define 2027—and how to invest in them

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Heraclitus, the Greek philosopher, is often credited with the idea that the only constant in life is change.
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2024, it appeared that pandemic-era inflation had been tamed, and the Federal Reserve responded with a series of cuts to its benchmark interest rate.
  • Industry observers note that this is glum news for homebuyers and the real estate industry, and for sectors including AI, which count on cheap credit to keep their businesses humming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heraclitus, the Greek philosopher, is often credited with the idea that the only constant in life is change. He was writing around 500 BC, but he could just as easily have been describing 2027, a year poised to bring seismic shifts in politics, technology, markets, and the way we live and work. Some of what’s coming is already in plain sight, like the AI revolution. Other forces are quieter but could prove just as consequential, including a likely surge in solar construction. Here are the five trends Fortune believes will define the coming year, and how investors can position themselves for each.

Recent findings suggest that in 2024, it appeared that pandemic-era inflation had been tamed, and the Federal Reserve responded with a series of cuts to its benchmark interest rate. This optimism didn’t last, however, and price shocks from tariffs and the Iran war led the Fed to boost rates in 2026. The central bank is expected to continue on this path.

Industry observers note that this is glum news for homebuyers and the real estate industry, and for sectors including AI, which count on cheap credit to keep their businesses humming. But high interest rates are not bad for everyone. Beneficiaries include individual savers, who can look forward to higher income, and major banks whose business involves lending money.

According to recent reports, while banks tend to earn more from loans when rates are higher, it is the “goliath” banks that do best in these environments, said Mike Mayo, head of U.S. large-cap bank research at Wells Fargo Securities. For 2027, Mayo said JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Bank of America (BAC), in particular, appear poised for a strong year based on bullish guidance they have issued. But he cautions that high interest rates only act as a tailwind up to a point—and that a rapid series of hikes would put larger portions of the economy under strain, counteracting the positive effect of higher interest rates for banks.

In a recent development, mayo dismissed concerns over new technologies, such as yield-seeking AI agents that could threaten the deposit base of the biggest banks such as Citigroup (C) and Wells Fargo (WFC). “The death of large banks has been exaggerated for 50 years,” he remarked. “Their deposit franchises have become bigger over time, and the reason is trust. Trust is more notable than Significant Tech.”.

Recent findings suggest that this trust in established financial institutions, along with big banks’ aversion to risk in general, are likely to serve the banks especially well at a time of mounting unease over cybersecurity—the result of a spate of recent incidents, including ones involving rogue AI agents. In this context, the “goliath” banks may draw investors looking for a safe and steady play.

And while their performance trailed the broader S&P 500 in 2026, the Major Four banks delivered on another attribute that investors value: large and reliable dividends.

Sources indicate that it’s been about four years since OpenAI’s launch of ChatGPT set off a massive rally in AI stocks. Some investors are getting jitters about the scope of the AI build-out amid fears that it’s a bubble—especially after the blue wave midterms elected a slew of Democrats on promises to rein in the AI industry. Still, the tech behemoths at the center of the boom—including Meta Platforms, Microsoft, and Amazon—are going full speed.

In a recent development, in this environment, looking for opportunities is not about deciding whether artificial intelligence is the future (spoiler alert: It is). The real question is which companies are positioned to succeed, no matter the pace of the AI build-out.

In this context, Bernstein senior analyst Stacy Rasgon likes the chipmaker Broadcom (AVGO) because its stock is “very, very cheap,” he told Fortune. The stock, like that of other chipmakers, sold off sharply in late 2026 as investors questioned how long the AI spending frenzy can last, even though earnings expectations remain strong.

Sources indicate that fellow chipmaker Nvidia’s shares took a major hit in November following revelations that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had acknowledged an affair, while the tech giant opened an investigation into reports that he had been targeted by Chinese intelligence. Huang resigned from the company he cofounded four days later.

Sources indicate that applied Materials (AMAT) is another stock that may offer considerable upside. The manufacturer sells equipment to manufacture chips, positioning Applied Materials to benefit from infrastructure investments in advanced processors, memory, and chip packaging. “It’s very clear to me that we need a lot more equipment,” stated Rasgon.

That doesn’t mean these companies won’t face potential headwinds in 2027. Arun Sundaram, an investment strategist at CFRA, points to potential energy bottlenecks and concerns that higher interest rates could make AI financing more expensive. He cites political pushback against data center construction as another potential obstacle—opposition that will only increase as Democrats, many of whom have been vocal critics of the AI industry, take power in Congress.

According to recent reports, still, analysts like Rasgon remain optimistic. He pointed to third-quarter earnings from Substantial Tech, which included more AI spending and a surge in cloud revenues. “As it turns out, a lot of these companies may be more profitable than people thought. They’re actually generating money,” he said. “From a fundamental level, we’ll probably see sustainability in spending … Whether or not sentiment from a stock standpoint is going to buy into that or not, I don’t know yet. But that’s going to be the key debate.”.

Most of our recommendations point you toward stocks or sectors to buy. When it comes to the defense industry in 2027 you might be well served to do the opposite: Stay on the sidelines. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine dragged into its fifth year in February 2026. That same month, the U.S. and Israel introduced a war against Iran, triggering retaliatory attacks across the Middle East. By early summer, there was anxious talk in Washington, D.C., about depleted stocks of missiles and other munitions.

In such an environment, investors might expect the shares of large defense companies to be soaring. That’s not the case. Even as demand for weapons has grown and a slew of techy startups have entered the sector, the stock prices of the big military contractors known as the “primes”—including RTX, Northrop Grumman, and General Dynamics—have largely flailed. Only one of these companies, Lockheed Martin, outperformed the S&P. Shares of Boeing, which has a sizable division that sells to the military, lagged the index by 30%.

High interest rates are glum news for homebuyers and the real estate and AI industries, but individual savers and major banks can benefit—up to a point.

The reason for this lackluster performance is ongoing uncertainty over U.S. defense spending, noted Peter Arment, a senior analyst at Baird. While the Pentagon and President Donald Trump are keen to pass a massive allocation for the military, it’s unclear where the money to pay for it would come from. Meanwhile, many in the incoming freshman class of Democrats vocally oppose Trump’s military policies.

While there is a tradition of bipartisan support for the military in Congress, this may not translate into a major defense bill in 2027, Arment said. Instead, lawmakers may rely on ad hoc measures that don’t include significant military spending.

It has been revealed that we’ve all heard the buzz about GLP-1s, the blockbuster category of drugs that are delivering dramatic results in treating obesity and Type 2 diabetes. In 2027, the medications—sold under brand names including Ozempic and Wegovy—are poised to reach even more patients as insurance coverage expands and pills offer an alternative to injections.

Recent findings suggest that JPMorgan forecasts that the global market for incretin-based drugs, which include GLP-1s, will reach $200 billion by 2030. In the U.S., the bank predicts that the number of patients taking these drugs will jump from roughly 10 million in 2025 to 25 million by the end of the decade.

Sources indicate that this rise will be driven in part by expanded Medicare access. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, which rolled out in July and runs through December 2027, offers certain weight-management drugs for $50 a month.

Sources indicate that GLP-1 in pill form could draw more users, too. Novo Nordisk’s oral Wegovy won FDA approval in December 2025, followed by Eli Lilly’s Foundayo in April 2026. Both are taken daily and could appeal to people who have held off on the treatment because they don’t like injections.

It has been revealed that lilly (LLY) and Novo (NVO) stocks stand to benefit the most. Both sell injectable and oral weight-loss treatments, and have spent years building the manufacturing facilities needed to meet demand. Lilly has committed more than $50 billion to U.S. manufacturing since 2020. It would take years for smaller would-be rivals to reach this scale. That business “moat” should help Lilly and Novo hold on to their lead, Evan Seigerman, BMO’s head of health care research, told Fortune: “I think that those two are poised to really maintain the lion’s share of the market in 2027,” he said. “You don’t see anyone else coming to take that share.”.

Industry observers note that for investors looking for a picks-and-shovels play outside of the drugmakers themselves, West Pharmaceutical Services (WST) is an option. The firm sells injectable-drug components like stoppers, plungers, and seals. Wall Street has taken notice: In November, Jefferies called the stock a buy and hiked its price target.

Those who assumed the solar sector was dead are missing out on one of the more surprising twists of 2027. Amid ongoing tensions in the Middle East, demand for energy is stronger than ever, and that is good news for solar power.

Solar companies are also poised to benefit from developers rushing to meet a key end-of-2027 deadline for federal clean-electricity tax credits. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 established the clean-electricity tax credits, but President Donald Trump’s 2025 One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act accelerated their expiration. Projects that began construction after July 4, 2026, must be placed in service by the end of 2027; those that began construction on or before that date can qualify even if they come online later, subject to other requirements. The investment credit generally covers 30% of qualifying costs for projects, with additional bonuses available. Developers can alternatively claim a credit based on electricity production.

A rush by solar installers to meet the end-of-2027 deadline is likely to boost sales for First Solar (FSLR), which makes electricity-generating panels, and for Nextpower (NXT) and Array Technologies (ARRY), which sell tracking systems that help panels follow the sun.

It has been revealed that regardless of how many installers meet the solar tax credit deadline, overall energy consumption will rise in 2027. UBS projects this will lead to 310 gigawatts of combined U.S. solar and wind additions through 2030, driven partly by power-hungry data centers and industrial customers. Goldman Sachs forecasts global data center power demand will rise 220% from 2023 levels by 2030.

Natural gas could help meet that demand, but there has been a surge in orders for the gas turbines that power data centers, meaning delivery can take years. Case in point: GE Vernova, a leading maker of this heavy-duty machinery, was already taking orders for 2031 in July 2026.

Those long lead times could give solar an opening. Gregory Nemet, a professor at the University of Wisconsin, told Fortune that developers planning data centers in the next few years may choose solar if they cannot get these turbines. “That dynamic is pretty consequential to how fast solar grows,” Nemet noted.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune.

#157601. Your Plan for Next Year Could Be in Trouble Before It Even Begins — Unless You Ask the Right Question

Your Plan for Next Year Could Be in Trouble Before It Even Begins — Unless You Ask the Right Question

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three fresh priorities competing for specialist capacity.
  • The planning baseline also highlighted an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the new year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three fresh priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

The planning baseline also highlighted an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the new year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

During the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the latest priorities to start as planned. The program lead mentioned the current end date still held unless the final regulatory review produced additional work. The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

What the planning discussion didn’t do was force the remediation work to compete again with the three latest priorities. It sat in the baseline as committed work, while leaders debated how to allocate what they believed was the remaining capacity.

By the end of the session, the team had made disciplined choices:.

The overcommitment was already there.

The problem became visible in the first weeks of execution. One of the approved priorities needed several of the same risk, legal and data specialists who were still closing the remediation program.

The planning model counted those people as partially available because the older work was expected to wind down early in the year. Instead, a final set of regulatory findings required more analysis, and a small group of specialists stayed fully engaged.

The new priority still had its approved funding, executive sponsor and start date. The people needed to move it weren’t actually free.

The old work was visible, but its claim on the upcoming year’s capacity had been treated as fixed background rather than as a choice.

Sources indicate that managers began stretching the same specialists across both commitments. The newly introduced priority’s first milestone slipped as specialist reviews that should have happened early were pushed behind remediation work. Meetings multiplied, decisions slowed, and work that looked fully staffed on paper started moving in fragments.

The pressure spread beyond those specialists. Project leads started moving milestones to fit the people they could get, finance held back some spending because dependent work couldn’t start, and senior leaders spent more time resolving clashes between commitments they believed had already been reconciled during planning.

The interesting thing was that the approved blueprint hadn’t changed, but the amount of work that could move at the same time already had.

According to recent reports, the new initiative hadn’t been badly prioritized at all. The leadership team had already removed a lower-ranked proposal, but part of the capacity used in the ranking exercise simply hadn’t been available to begin with.

This is where the “Hidden Problems” execution leak appears.

The planning process had surfaced the remediation program, its budget and its expected completion date, yet the upcoming work was still being ranked against an overstated view of what remained available.

A baseline records what’s already in motion, but it doesn’t force old work to justify its capacity against new work. Once carryover is treated as given, only the new initiatives are asked to compete.

That distinction matters because visibility can create false confidence.

Leaders can see every major piece of work on one page and still never face the question of whether an old commitment deserves to keep the people and budget it carried across the year boundary.

In a recent development, listing carryover isn’t the same as choosing it again. The planning process therefore becomes disciplined about one side of the load while leaving the other side untouched.

When execution starts slowly, leadership tightens prioritization. Leaders ask for fewer initiatives, sharper business cases and clearer ranking, then delay or reject new proposals that can’t justify scarce capacity.

In a recent development, those actions improve the choices among new priorities; however, they don’t reopen the older commitments already sitting in the baseline. That was the pattern in this business unit.

Leadership had reduced the newly introduced-priority list before approving the strategy, and when capacity pressure appeared, the first response was to ask whether one of the new initiatives should move more slowly.

The remediation program wasn’t part of that debate because it had been approved in the prior year, and finishing it was treated as an “obligation” rather than as a competing use of scarce capacity.

The organization was re-ranking newly introduced work while the carryover never faced the same test.

According to recent reports, A stronger planning process adds a formal carryover line. That certainly improves visibility, but it doesn’t change the underlying mechanism when carryover remains exempt from comparison.

The remediation work can appear clearly in the initiative, with its budget, owner and expected completion date, and still never face the one central question: Is finishing this work now more valuable than starting the new priority that needs the same people?

Industry observers note that in this business unit, the remediation program remained on every planning view. Its existence was never hidden. What did stay hidden was the effect of treating its capacity claim as “non-negotiable” while the latest priorities competed for whatever was left.

The initiative could be complete as an inventory and incomplete as a capacity decision.

Every item appeared somewhere, but not every item had to earn its place in the same contest for scarce people and budget.

According to recent reports, by the time the conflict became obvious, leaders were dealing with a problem the planning process had already created. The remediation work couldn’t simply stop, and the new priority had already been approved.

According to recent reports, the same scarce specialists now sat between two legitimate commitments, each with consequences for delay. Leaders were forced to make the tradeoff during execution instead of during planning, when they still had more room to change the portfolio.

When that conflict reached the next leadership review, the discussion was no longer about which work deserved to start. It was about which already-approved commitment would lose access to people both sides now depended on.

In a recent development, the plan didn’t fail because leaders chose the wrong fresh priorities. Not at all. The planning choice had been postponed until both commitments were already in motion.

Sources indicate that A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three upcoming priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

It has been revealed that the planning baseline also revealed an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the newly introduced year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

During the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the new priorities to start as planned. The program lead remarked the current end date still held unless the final regulatory review produced additional work. The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

Recent findings suggest that the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator highlights today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.

Sources indicate that A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

According to recent reports, on November 6, the same day Elon Musk announced the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

Sources indicate that latest inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search revealed no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

If there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

Sources indicate that but the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”.

Recent findings suggest that that’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

In a recent development, some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t said whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

This is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we said it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

The past weeks have seen the broad crypto ETF market face consistent withdrawals from investors, causing Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, and others to record steady outflows since October.

While the negative trend has continued, Solana has just taken over the leadership in the broad ETF market after recording its first inflow in a while.

Latest data from SosoValue shows that while Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP ETFs have continued to struggle with consistent weekly outflows, Solana has just beaten the trend after it finally ended a six-week streak of consecutive weekly outflows.

Notably, the data shows that Solana spot ETFs have recorded a net inflow of $4.38 million over the week.

Although the net amount of capital received by the ETFs appears decent, it is significant considering the growing crypto market weakness.

While this marks an end to the Solana ETFs' six-week outflow streak, this is the first positive weekly performance they have recorded since October 9.

Further data demonstrates that Bitcoin spot ETFs suffered the largest withdrawals as investors pulled out about $1.79 billion during the same period.

The negative trend also extended to the Ethereum ETF market as the funds posted a total of $314.17 million in net outflows following the consistent selling pressure.

In addition to this, the XRP spot ETFs were not spared, as the funds recorded $11.11 million in weekly outflows, leaving Solana as the only one among the four major crypto ETFs to finish the week on a positive note.

#157596. I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1099 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Industry observers note that the bonus was simple.
  • After it started, creative quality dropped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that the bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

The target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the blueprint asked for.

I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

In a recent development, for a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

We traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

In a recent development, when we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. New editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

Sources indicate that that changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

Sources indicate that I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

Bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

Industry observers note that we stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

The results came promptly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

Sources indicate that the difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

Recent findings suggest that we’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

Recent findings suggest that the early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

Recent findings suggest that while the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

The hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Sources indicate that before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

In a recent development, if you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

Sources indicate that the bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.
