Industry News: AI boom or bust? 10 under-the-radar stock picks and investing ideas for either scenario

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that investors don’t have to decide whether AI will change the world.
  • According to recent reports, the same goes if the bubble bursts—a risk that Nvidia’s recent troubles heighten.
  • To help navigate both sides of the trade, Fortune has identified six investment strategies for 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that investors don’t have to decide whether AI will change the world. They do, however, have to determine how much of their portfolio should depend on it. After all, AI bets now extend far beyond the obvious megacap tech stocks. Utilities and power-equipment makers have been swept up in the data center build-out. Even parts of the energy sector now trade on the promise that AI will consume an enormous amount of electricity.

According to recent reports, the same goes if the bubble bursts—a risk that Nvidia’s recent troubles heighten. Because classic AI stocks are weighted so heavily in indexes like the S&P 500, even a standard 60/40 portfolio can mean betting big on this nascent technology. Investors looking to hedge must find something that doesn’t depend on the very boom they’re worried about.

To help navigate both sides of the trade, Fortune has identified six investment strategies for 2027. Three are built to ride the boom—and three will help you survive a bust.

The VanEck Data Center Supply Chain ETF allocates to companies that help power, operate, and equip data centers. It’s a bet on the physical infrastructure of the AI boom rather than solely the hyperscalers and software developers themselves.

Industry observers note that that’s because the fund gives investors exposure to several layers of the data center supply chain. Think chipmakers, along with companies that make notable computing components, like Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, and Micron. Industrial companies like Eaton, Vertiv, and Johnson Controls that provide the electrical equipment and cooling solutions for these energy-intensive facilities are included as well. Meanwhile, Quanta Services and Amphenol add exposure to the construction and connectivity themes.

Tom Essaye, founder of Sevens Report Research, likened the broadening AI trade to “water sweeping across a floor,” reaching “places that people would not think had anything to do with AI.”.

Bryan Armour, director of ETF and passive strategies research for North America at Morningstar, points to RACK as a way to look beyond traditional tech funds and growth stocks to capitalize on the AI trade. “You need to build the data centers, you need to build the chips and the GPUs and memory and all the different components,” Armour noted.

The Roundhill Neocloud ETF bets on the landlords of AI computing: businesses that build specialized data centers packed with GPUs and rent out the processing power AI companies need to train and run their models.

In a recent development, two neocloud providers, Nebius and CoreWeave, make up more than half of the fund; many of the rest have been in Bitcoin mining and are retooling for AI. The bet is that rising demand for computing will fill up these facilities and lead to upcoming contracts.

Sources indicate that the Roundhill Photonics & Optics ETF (LYTE) and the KraneShares Photonic and Optical ETF (LUMA) both target a key bottleneck in the AI build-out: moving enormous amounts of data promptly and efficiently. Both funds offer exposure to companies developing optical technologies that increase bandwidth and reduce the energy needed to move information between chips and across data centers as AI computing demands grow.

These ETFs invest in the suppliers behind those connections. LYTE holds stocks such as Ciena and Eoptolink, while KraneShares’ LUMA counts LandMark Optoelectronics, Soitec, and Marvell among its major holdings.

Sources indicate that “AI will still have legs next year,” said Todd Rosenbluth, head of research at VettaFi. “There will still be demand for companies that offer [this] exposure.”.

It has been revealed that still, investors allocating to these more specialized funds must be prepared: All the names here rolled out in 2026, so they don’t have long track records and tend to swoon when the AI trade comes under pressure. “The narrower you invest in the market,” Rosenbluth remarked, “the greater the volatility.”.

Think the AI boom is overheated? These strategies can help hedge your portfolio if the AI trade falls back to earth.

The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF offers a straightforward way to loosen AI’s grip on your portfolio. Unlike the traditional S&P 500 index, which gives the biggest companies the largest weighting, RSP resets its holdings to equal weighting each quarter. That puts chipmaking giant Nvidia on par with any other company at each quarterly rebalance. If megacap tech underperforms while the rest of the market holds up, RSP could lose less than the traditional S&P 500 index. That stated, for the first nine months of 2026, RSP returned roughly 9.9%, including reinvested dividends, lagging the broad-market index’s 12.7% total return.

The Invesco S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) buys the 100 S&P 500 stocks with the smallest price swings over the previous 12 months. SPLV can offset some AI risk because the fund allocates to seemingly steadier businesses, rather than companies with exceptionally high growth expectations. The fund has little exposure to Massive Tech and much larger allocations to utilities, financials, and real estate. Because SPLV counts utilities among its holdings, however, it’s not completely AI-free.

Sources indicate that although SPLV lagged the S&P 500 during the first nine months of 2026, it remained positive for the year through Sept. 30. The fund provided some downside cushioning in 2022, when the Federal Reserve started aggressively hiking interest rates. That year, in total returns, the S&P 500 dropped 18.1%, while SPLV fell only 4.9%.

Sources indicate that the iShares Core High Dividend ETF (HDV) targets high-paying dividend stocks. The appeal is less “this manufacturer could change the world” and more “this company can pay shareholders now.” Investors who want a stake in established businesses rather than expectations of explosive growth might consider HDV. It’s been a banner year for the fund, with a strong first nine months in 2026. Including reinvested dividends, HDV returned approximately 17.5%, beating the S&P 500’s total return of 12.75%.

It has been revealed that the strategy is not foolproof, though. Companies can cut their dividends, and the fund can dive with the broader market; however, it can be a different and welcome source of returns.

According to recent reports, the Vanguard Morningstar Value ETF (VTV) invests in large-cap stocks that are considered relatively inexpensive against their business fundamentals. Where the AI trade often asks investors to pay up for future growth, value investing means finding assets that are trading for less than their intrinsic worth. That makes VTV a potential hedge if the market sours on these growth stocks.

JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway, ExxonMobil, and Johnson & Johnson are among the fund’s holdings, as well as a smattering of tech names like Micron. For the first nine months of 2026, VTV returned approximately 14.8%.

Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities offer a hedge against a less obvious risk of the AI boom: that building the future makes everything more expensive. A massive build-out of data centers, power plants, and transmission lines could weigh on supplies of equipment and skilled labor. That can push inflation higher.

These government bonds adjust their principal with the consumer price index. Their fixed interest rate applies to that adjusted balance, meaning payments rise alongside inflation. Investors can access TIPS through funds such as the Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF (VTIP) and the iShares TIPS Bond ETF (TIP). Although both lagged the S&P 500 during the first nine months of 2026, when inflation was rampant they held up much better. (In 2022, on a total return basis, including distributions, the S&P 500 tumbled more than 18%, while VTIP and TIP shed roughly 3% and 12%, respectively.).

VettaFi’s Rosenbluth warns that inflation is not in the rearview mirror, in his opinion. “The environment we’re in today, where companies are spending a lot to support artificial intelligence, that can and has been contributing to inflation being elevated.”.

Industry observers note that for Rosenbluth, that concern fits into a broader challenge for 2027, when some view this breakthrough technology as overhyped and others believe it’s still in the early stages. Making sure a portfolio has room for more than one outcome is key.

Recent findings suggest that “Everyone is long AI,” he stated. The priority is “just having a balanced portfolio, because there’s just such a wide range of potential outcomes next year.”.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 glitch of Fortune.

Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that daily pool data reveals Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that daily pool data reveals Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

It has been revealed that according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

It has been revealed that zecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

In a recent development, across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

Industry observers note that at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

In a recent development, the deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

Recent findings suggest that NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

In a recent development, ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest patch on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In a recent development, in October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

It has been revealed that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

According to recent reports, the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

From dorm delivery robots to real‑world video games, UW students show off inventions

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.
  • Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering.
  • But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club indicated that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.

Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club indicated that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

“We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya said. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”.

It has been revealed that CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Recent findings suggest that twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

According to recent reports, “We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu mentioned. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”.

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

In a recent development, “The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya noted. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”.

According to recent reports, according to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry said have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry mentioned.

In a recent development, other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

In a recent development, “Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”.

In a recent development, his team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

Other inventions sought to get owners off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

“I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae stated. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”.

Recent findings suggest that also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

In a recent development, “The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev said. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”.

Recent findings suggest that his prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he plans to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

Recent findings suggest that “We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards said. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”.

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:.

This cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

Sources indicate that to do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

“We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat stated. “Maybe even globally.”.

Veteran trader Peter Brandt has softened the tone of his recent Bitcoin warnings and said on X that the cryptocurrency held at the level it needed to hold after its drop to $55,150 over the weekend.

"Bitcoin held exactly where it had to hold -- for now anyway, but perhaps for more than now," Brandt wrote on Monday.

It has been revealed that brandt also shared a monthly chart of Bitcoin together with the post. The chart goes back to 2018, and Brandt marked on it the same patterns that he had already pointed to in previous years. According to the chart, the price of Bitcoin was back above $63,000 at the time of the post and stood at $63,338.

According to recent reports, on Saturday, Bitcoin fell as low as $55,150. It was the lowest price of the cryptocurrency since September 2024, and before that, the lowest price of Bitcoin in 2026 was $57,718 on July 1, according to Coinbase.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 15, Brandt posted a weekly chart with a possible head-and-shoulders top and said that, if the pattern proves valid, Bitcoin's October 2025 record of about $126,000 may not be surpassed in his lifetime. Two days before that, on Nov. 13, Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 for the first time since August.

Recent findings suggest that brandt has also pointed to the history of Bitcoin's bull market cycles more than once. Late last year, he posted a chart showing that each of Bitcoin's five major bull runs began after drawdowns of 75% or more, and he wrote that if the decline carried to $50,000, "the next bull market cycle should carry to $200k to $250K.".

Sources indicate that in April, Brandt remarked that Bitcoin could form an "investable low" in September or October 2026. According to Brandt, this low may or may not go below the February low near $60,000, and the next cycle peak could land between $300,000 and $500,000 in September or October 2029 if the four-year cycle continues to hold.

"Real bottom will not occur until October 2026," Brandt noted in an interview in February.

In a recent development, the latest Brandt post comes amid a rally in U.S. tech stocks on Monday. Earlier that day, Nvidia revealed that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer and board member, effective immediately.

It has been revealed that according to the Nvidia announcement, the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government before the decision, and it is confident that Huang's return "poses no national security risk." Shares of Nvidia surged 33% after the news, according to CNBC.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin went up together with tech stocks and briefly climbed above $64,000 on Monday. Before the Nvidia news, Bitcoin had already recovered from the Saturday low to around $61,500.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12. On Nov. 17, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

Industry observers note that as the workday progresses, you face small problems. Your phone is almost dead, with no charger in sight. You can’t find the piece of paper with yesterday’s meeting notes.

None of these small issues necessitates a complete office makeover. Sometimes you just need a small upgrade to make life easier, like a charging station for your devices, a lamp that puts light where you need it or a voice recorder that transcribes meetings for you.

According to recent reports, black Friday is one of the best times to shop for office technology. The right purchase can remove everyday irritations — or simply make your workspace more pleasant — at a discounted price.

Sources indicate that the selections below cover ten different uses of technology, all confirmed Black Friday bargains. The aim is a better-equipped office.

In a recent development, tired of taking meeting notes? Let AI do it for you. The Pocket AI voice recorder captures every word of a meeting and offers a transcript as well as an AI summary in the app. It lasts up to four days on a single charge. The only downside is that without a premium subscription, recordings only last 30 days in the app. The subscription costs $30 per month for unlimited summaries and the highest-quality transcription. Pocket has sold more than 200,000 devices so far. A Black Friday deal brings the price of the recorder down 25% from $159 to $119.

Recent findings suggest that former Twitter engineers Abdur Chowdhury and Eric Jensen debuted Aura in 2016 to help families connect through shared photos. The device has been popular every year around the holidays as a meaningful gift. Multiple people can connect to a picture frame and send images and videos to the frame via text or through the app. They can also preload photos, videos or messages to the frame before gifting. Aura doesn’t charge storage or subscription fees, so users can upload unlimited images. The 10-inch picture frame is 41% off for Black Friday, so it costs $139 instead of $234.

According to recent reports, everyone in an office or home environment can add their events and schedules directly on this smart calendar. They can instantly synchronize their schedules and collaborate, drawing data from sources like Google Calendar and Outlook. Consumers simply plug in, connect to Wi-Fi and sync their calendars within a few minutes. The calendar’s design allows it to easily fit on a table, countertop or wall, and it has a 15-inch touchscreen display. On Black Friday, the price drops from $320 to $270, a 16% reduction.

It has been revealed that turn an office chore into a manageable project. The label maker connects through Bluetooth and offers an app with templates for creating labels. The product is a practical option for naming drawers and identifying supplies. It brings consistency to a filing system and is small enough to slip into your pocket. Entrepreneurs can use it to create price tags for their products. Amazon’s 30% Black Friday discount brings the price of this label maker down to about $16. It was previously $23.

This speaker looks like a miniature desktop computer. It has a customizable 1.77-inch pixel screen that can display over 70 retro clock faces and animations. Owners can set alarms on the speaker, play white noise or rain sounds and set timers and reminders. All of this happens on the screen, so users can stop bringing their phones to bed if they don’t want distractions. They can also stream music over Bluetooth or connect by USB to their laptops, with no need for Wi-Fi. The speaker is 20% off for Black Friday, dropping from $60 to $48, a 365-day low price.

This device allows someone to indicate to others in the office that they are busy at work and should not be interrupted. The LED pixel display can show a busy message, along with a timer that reveals how long the employee needs to focus. The screen securely attaches to the top of a monitor or fits on a desk. Consumers can control the device via an app and mute notifications promptly from the app. The message syncs across devices, like laptops, smartphones and smartwatches. The typical price is $219, but the device is discounted 27% for Black Friday, bringing the price down to $159.

Acer 7-in-1 wireless charging station.

It’s a charging station perfect for desks cluttered with Apple devices. The station works with compatible iPhones, Apple Watches and AirPods. It removes the need to find outlets for multiple devices and eliminates the clutter of cables. The device also has a smart LED clock and night light that feature four adjustable brightness levels. The list price for the charging station is $80, but it is 41% off for Black Friday, bringing the price down to $47.

The LED desk lamp offers a practical upgrade to any desk setup. It has 25 light combination modes with five different color temperatures and brightness levels, and offers night light and reading settings. Users control the lamp with a wireless smart remote control, switching between modes and brightness levels. The dual heads bring light to desks with widths of up to 71 inches. The lamp clamps to desk edges. A Black Friday deal of 36% off brings the price down from $70 to $44.

Industry observers note that charge multiple devices simultaneously through three outlets and four USB ports. To be more specific, it has two USB-C ports, two USB-A ports and three AC outlets. The power strip clamps to the edge of a desk. The table needs to be about half an inch away from the wall and a maximum of 1.96 inches thick to fit the clamp. The price of this device dropped from $25 to $21 for Black Friday.

Recent findings suggest that looking for the perfect decorative addition to any work desk? This levitating globe floats between two magnets at the top and bottom of the frame. It comes with an LED light feature that makes it stand out in the dark. It could spark conversations with colleagues and it is also simple to set up. Black Friday brings the price of this novelty object below $30. It was originally $37 but is now 19% off and costs around $29.

Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.
  • On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still states Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.
  • Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still states Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Recent findings suggest that embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It notes: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no latest burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Recent findings suggest that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the organization wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide states "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

Sources indicate that the main text above it claims something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

Industry observers note that as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

Industry observers note that the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

In a recent development, for teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

Recent findings suggest that for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

Copilot without M365, and more news you didn’t hear (but maybe should have) at Microsoft Ignite

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.
  • Sources indicate that many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week.
  • Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.

Sources indicate that many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week. But not all the newly introduced goodies confirmed there (or simultaneous with this year’s Microsoft Ignite show, which kicked off Nov. 17) might have made it onto everyone’s radar.

Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365. But there was some other important news last week that Microsoft customers could find equally, if not more, interesting and useful.

Among my picks for the “make sure you didn’t miss this” list:.

Recent findings suggest that copilot without the M365 subscription prerequisite arrives next week: Despite a LOT of talk about Copilot, “a new OS for work,” Microsoft didn’t mention anything at all during Ignite about a new purchasing option for Copilot that is set to go live on Dec. 1. Starting then, Microsoft will offer a version of Copilot to small business and enterprise customers without the current prerequisite of having a certain paid Microsoft 365 blueprint.

For a flat fee of $21 per user per month for small businesses and $30 per user per month for enterprise customers (before discounts), users will be able to buy this fresh standalone Copilot offering, as Microsoft quietly announced back in October on its Partner Center site.

It has been revealed that presently, to buy Copilot, business customers need to have purchased a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription strategy before they shell out even more money for Copilot. Because of this requirement, Microsoft isn’t competitive price-wise when pitted against OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude entry-level business tiers.

The new offer is for new customers buying through any of Microsoft’s channels, including its Cloud Solution Provider program, across commercial, education, government and nonprofit sectors.

I’ve got a lot of questions about this newly introduced offer, including where Copilot chats are stored and how/if customers will get some kind of access to the Microsoft IQ technology that underlies Copilot and is positioned as its secret sauce if they don’t have a Microsoft 365 subscription. I’ve asked Microsoft, but no word back so far.

Azure Linux 4.0 is now ready for prime time: Revealed on the same day Ignite kicked off (but without a mention during the conference), Microsoft’s own commercial Linux distribution, Azure Linux 4.0, is now generally available.

The 4.0 release is interesting for a few reasons. First, it is the first release of Azure Linux — formerly known as Common Base Linux (CBL)-Mariner — designed as a general-purpose server OS for customer virtual machines, and it is based on the Fedora Linux stack. Checking off the requisite AI box, Azure Linux 4.0 is “purpose-built for cloud native and AI workloads,” as Microsoft said back in May.

It has been revealed that microsoft officials have mentioned two-thirds of customer cores in Azure run Linux (not Windows Server). Microsoft has acknowledged the platforms running Microsoft 365, GitHub and OpenAI’s ChatGPT “all sit on Linux foundations.”.

Microsoft has supported a wide variety of Linux distributions on Azure for years but never made its own available for commercial use by customers and partners until now.

According to recent reports, windows Server 2028 is in the works: Yes, another on-premises version of Windows Server is coming. Christened Windows Server 2028, the next release, likely to debut in late 2027, is now in public preview.

Microsoft mentioned Server 2028 in its Book of News and in passing in some sessions, but it was not positioned as a top-tier announcement.

The 2028 release includes some expected and a few surprise features, such as making 32-bit app support an optional component rather than installing it by default. That change, along with a hardened Server Core configuration included by default, is designed to improve the security of the platform from the get-go. But they may present potential backward-compatibility risks.

Microsoft is positioning Server 2028 similarly to the way it has been pushing Windows client lately: as a way to run AI workloads more cheaply because they can run locally. The “unmetered intelligence” pitch strikes again.

Sources indicate that sure, Microsoft can’t make every announcement a centerpiece in a two-plus-hour (waah!) opening keynote. But sometimes, hidden gems deserve their moments in the sun. Or pouring rain ….
